entry.title: Ship the image you tested: build once, promote, roll back

link.title: Ship the image you tested: build once, promote, roll back

entry.content:
In June we moved our chatbot’s production environment to a newer model. The pull request changed two lines in each of two config files: the model deployment name and the model name, for UAT and for production. No Python file changed.

It still went to production the same way a code change does. It merged, deployed to UAT, got a version tag and waited for an approval. Then the production deploy copied an image that UAT had already run, and pointed the cluster at it together with the new config. Nothing was built for production.

This post is about that release model. You build the container image once, name it after the commit, and move that exact image from one environment to the next. Everything that differs between environments stays outside the image. This is usually called image promotion, or “build once, deploy many”. To roll back, you point back at an older image. I’ll go through how our pipeline does it, where it still falls short, and what an LLM service adds. I’ll leave out the names of registries, repositories and models, which aren’t mine to share.

A build, a release and a run

The Twelve-Factor App splits shipping into three stages [1]. The build turns code into an executable bundle. The release combines that build with the config of one deploy. The run starts the release in its environment. Every release has a unique ID and is never changed after it is created. If you need a change, you make a new release.

For a container service, the build is the image. The release is the image plus one environment’s config. In our setup, a release is one commit in a Git repo that Argo CD watches. More on that below.

Why not build again for each environment? Humble and Farley answer it in Continuous Delivery: “Every time you compile the code, you run the risk of introducing some difference” [2]. A rebuild can pick up a newer base image, a newer system package or a different tool version. Then production runs an image nobody tested. They call binaries built for one environment “a very bad practice” [2].

What our pipeline does

We have three environments: dev, UAT and production. A deploy goes through three repos. The app repo has small workflows that run tests and start a deploy. A shared repo holds the reusable workflows that do the dispatch. A separate infra repo builds the image, pushes it to the registry and updates the Kubernetes manifests. Argo CD watches the infra repo and applies it to the cluster.

Each environment has its own trigger:

  • A merge into development runs smoke tests, then builds an image and deploys it to dev.
  • A promotion PR from development into main builds a fresh image from main and deploys it to UAT. A small workflow fills the PR body with the list of commits it carries.
  • A version tag such as v1.4.0 on main deploys to production. A person must approve it in a GitHub environment first. Then the infra repo copies the UAT image into the production registry with az acr import and pins the manifest to it.

Before it asks for approval, the production workflow checks that the tagged commit is on main and has an exact version tag.

Try it below. Step one change through the three environments, then roll it back. Then tick the rebuild box and run it again. The SHAs and digests are made up.

One change, from merge to rollback

Each panel shows the image an environment runs: its tag, the digest of its bytes, and where it came from.

DEV
UAT
PRODUCTION
INFRA REPO, DEPLOY COMMITS

    Where we stopped short

    Our design record for this, ADR-002, describes a stricter version. It builds once, when code merges into development, and promotes that one image to UAT and then to production. The record still has the status “Proposed”. The workflows went a different way, and UAT gets its own build.

    The merge commit is one reason this is hard. A promotion PR into main creates a new commit with a new SHA. The code is the same, but the name is not. So the dev image and the UAT image are two builds with two names.

    So in our pipeline, “build once” holds from UAT to production and not from dev to UAT. UAT to production is the step that matters most, because production must run what the testers saw. Two things in our Dockerfile make the second build less risky. The Python base image is pinned by digest, and dependencies come from a lock file with uv sync --frozen. One step still installs system packages without a version, so two builds of the same code can still differ a little.

    Microsoft’s guide to image tags makes the same point about git SHAs. It calls a git commit tag “semi-stable”, because a rebuild of the same commit can pick up a new base image [5].

    Name the image after the commit

    Every image is tagged with the 7-character git SHA of the commit it was built from. ADR-001 compared this with semantic versions, build numbers and timestamps. The SHA won because any workflow can compute it from its own checkout. The build and deploy workflows don’t need to pass a version between them. And git show a1b2c3d shows exactly what is running.

    Each build also gets a second tag with the environment name, such as :uat. That tag moves on every deploy. It is only there for people browsing the registry. The manifests always pin the SHA tag.

    The running app also needs to say what it is. The deploy step writes an APP_VERSION variable into the manifest: the short SHA on dev and UAT, the release tag on production. The app reports it on a /version endpoint and in a response header. We dropped our release tool in June. The version in pyproject.toml is now a fixed 0.0.0, and the deploy is the only source of the version.

    A tag is still only a name. The Kubernetes documentation says: “Tags can be moved to point to different images, but digests are fixed” [4]. A digest is the SHA-256 hash of the image manifest. If a manifest pins app@sha256:..., the cluster runs the same bytes even if someone pushes a new image under the old tag. We pin tags, and they stay fixed by convention. Nothing in the workflows I read locks them.

    Config stays outside the image

    If one image runs everywhere, everything that differs must come from outside: endpoints, model deployment names, index names, log levels and secrets. Twelve-Factor defines config as “everything that is likely to vary between deploys” [1].

    Ours lives in the app repo, in one plain YAML file per environment:

    # config/uat.yaml (values are placeholders)
ENVIRONMENT: "uat"
LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME: "chat-primary"
MODEL_FALLBACK_DEPLOYMENT_NAME: "chat-fallback"
AI_SEARCH_INDEX_NAME: "docs-live"
AI_SEARCH_EVAL_INDEX_NAME: "docs-eval-frozen"

    Secrets never go in this file. They live in a key vault, and an ExternalSecret resource in the infra repo pulls them into the cluster.

    At deploy time, the infra workflow copies these values into the environment’s ConfigMap. Here is a simplified sketch of one production deploy, not the exact workflow:

    SHA=e4f5a6b
yq -i ".spec.template.spec.containers[0].image = \"registry.example.com/app:$SHA\"" \
  k8s/prod/deployment.yaml
# also set APP_VERSION=v1.4.0 in the same manifest
yq -i '.data = load("source/config/prod.yaml")' k8s/prod/configmap.yaml
# if the ConfigMap changed, bump an annotation on the pod template
git commit -am "deploy(prod): app:$SHA" && git push   # Argo CD syncs from here

    The annotation is needed because a Deployment doesn’t restart its pods when a ConfigMap changes. Helm’s docs show the usual fix: put a checksum of the ConfigMap in the pod template, so a config change also changes the template [6]. Ours writes a timestamp instead, and only when the config changed.

    Two of our choices differ from the textbook. First, Twelve-Factor says not to group config into named environments, because that “does not scale cleanly” [1]. We do group it, in three files. With three fixed environments, that has been fine so far.

    Second, the config file comes from the same commit as the image. So the image and its config go through review and promotion together. Google’s SRE book describes this option: teams “snapshot and release configuration files alongside their binaries”. It also warns that config read from the head of the main branch “often leads to skew” with what is running [3].

    The cost is that every config change needs a commit, a new SHA and a new release. The model change at the top of this post went through UAT and a version tag like any code change. I think that is right for an LLM service. One config line can change the model, and that changes behaviour as much as code does.

    What a version means for an LLM service

    For a plain web service, the image SHA and the config describe most of what runs. An LLM service has more parts that change.

    Prompts are code. Ours are TOML files in the image, one per model, picked by the model name in config. So a config change that switches the model needs the prompt file for that model to be in the image already. The image has to ship first, or in the same release.

    Deployment names differ between environments. The same model can have one deployment name in dev and another in production. That is why the name is config, and the prompt is picked by model name instead of deployment name.

    The knowledge base changes without a deploy. The search index is refreshed on its own schedule, so the same image and config can give a different answer next week. Our /version endpoint returns three fields for this reason:

    { "version": "v1.4.0", "kb_index": "docs-live", "kb_version": "2026-10-20T03:00:12Z" }

    kb_version is the end time of the indexer’s last run. For evaluation, a request header switches retrieval to a frozen copy of the index, made by a manual workflow. Then /version reports the frozen index and the kb_version it was copied from. An eval score can be tied to one image, one config and one corpus.

    Gates between environments

    Promotion only helps if something checks the image before the next step. Ours, in order:

    • A pull request into development runs unit tests, with no model calls.
    • A pull request into main runs the full suite, including all the tests that call the model.
    • Every dev and UAT deploy runs smoke tests first, which include a few real model calls. If they fail, the deploy is skipped.
    • After a deploy, someone can run a deployment verification test by hand against dev or UAT. It checks health, asks a question, sends feedback, asks a follow-up that depends on the first answer, and sends a malformed request. A model then judges whether the follow-up used the first turn.
    • Production needs a person to approve it.

    There is no automated quality score between UAT and production yet. The approval is where a person looks at the evidence.

    Rollback is a git revert

    Every deploy is one commit in the infra repo. That commit changes the image pin, APP_VERSION and the ConfigMap together. So rollback is a git revert of that commit, and Argo CD syncs the cluster back. Our rollback workflow asks for the environment, an optional infra commit, and the word YES.

    This is also what Argo CD expects. Its docs say “Rollback cannot be performed against an application with automated sync enabled” [7]. Git is the source of truth, so the undo happens in Git. A side effect is a free deploy log: git log -- k8s/prod/deployment.yaml lists every production release.

    A revert only undoes what is in that commit. It doesn’t undo a refreshed knowledge base, or data that the new release wrote in a new shape. If a release changes what the app stores between turns, the older image must still be able to read it, or the rollback breaks open conversations.

    An LLM step in CI should fail soft

    One small story. Our promotion PRs used to start with a generated summary. A workflow step sent the commit list to a hosted model and wrote a short summary into the PR body. At some point the model API began to answer with HTTP 410, Gone.

    The step had been written to degrade. On any status other than 200, it wrote one line instead: “AI summary unavailable (HTTP 410). See raw commits below.” So the promotion PRs still opened and deploys were never blocked. However, that line sat at the top of every promotion PR from late August until 22 October. Then we removed the step and kept the plain commit list.

    A model call in CI is a call to a service you don’t control. Make it optional, as this one was. But a soft failure is also a quiet one. If nothing reports it, it can stay broken for weeks.

    Things to watch

    • Environment tags move. Tags like :uat point somewhere new on every deploy. Never deploy from them.
    • Short SHAs can clash. Our infra build named the tag with git rev-parse --short=7, which adds characters when 7 are ambiguous. The promotion cut the full SHA to exactly 7. In the rare case of a clash, the two would disagree.
    • Tagging a commit UAT never built. Production copies an existing image. On purpose, a merge into main builds nothing unless it comes from development or a hotfix branch. If you tag one of those, there is nothing to copy, and the promotion fails.
    • A break-glass path. We keep a manual workflow that deploys to dev with Helm directly, for when the infra repo or Argo CD is down. That deploy is not in Git. Redeploy through the normal path once it is back.
    • Moving workflow references. Our callers use the shared workflows at @v1, a tag that moves with each release of the shared repo. Until July they used @main. GitHub’s hardening guide recommends a full commit SHA, because “a tag can be moved or deleted” [8]. @v1 trades some of that safety for getting fixes without editing every caller.
    • Config ahead of the image. A config value that needs code the image doesn’t have yet fails at runtime, not at build time. Ship the code first.

    What I would try next

    Reading how others do this showed me a few things our pipeline doesn’t do yet.

    • Promote the dev image to UAT. If main took the exact commit from development instead of a new merge commit, the SHA would stay the same. Then UAT could copy the dev image. Today the promotion PR is merged with a merge commit, so this needs a change in how we merge.
    • Pin by digest. Record the digest at build time and pin app@sha256:... in the manifests. The SHA tag can stay for people [4].
    • Lock deployed tags. Microsoft’s guide recommends locking every deployed tag, by setting write-enabled to false, as a step in the release pipeline [5].
    • Build provenance. SLSA provenance is a record of how an artifact was built: which builder, which inputs and which dependencies [9]. With it, production could check that an image came from our pipeline before it runs.
    • An eval gate before the tag. Run the golden set against the frozen index on UAT, and put the scores next to the approval. I wrote about golden datasets before.

    If you run an LLM service on Kubernetes, start with two rules. Tag each image with its commit and never build for production. Then make each deploy one commit that pins the image and its config together, so a rollback is one revert.

    References

    1. The Twelve-Factor App, sections “Build, release, run” and “Config”. The three stages, release IDs, and config as everything that varies between deploys.
    2. Jez Humble and David Farley, “Continuous Delivery: Anatomy of the Deployment Pipeline”, excerpt from Continuous Delivery, Addison-Wesley, 2010. “Only build your binaries once”, and why binaries should not be environment-specific.
    3. Dinah McNutt, “Release Engineering”, in Site Reliability Engineering, Google, 2016. Hermetic builds, build IDs, and the ways to ship configuration with or apart from binaries.
    4. Kubernetes, “Images”. Tags against digests, pinning an image by digest, and avoiding :latest.
    5. Microsoft, “Image tag best practices”, Azure Container Registry. Stable against unique tags, git commits as “semi-stable” tags, and locking deployed tags.
    6. Helm, “Chart development tips and tricks”, section “Automatically Roll Deployments”. The checksum annotation that restarts pods when a ConfigMap changes.
    7. Argo CD, “Automated sync policy”. Self-heal and prune are off by default, and rollback is not possible with automated sync on.
    8. GitHub, “Security hardening for GitHub Actions”. Pinning actions to a full commit SHA instead of a tag.
    9. SLSA, “Provenance”, specification v1.0. What a build provenance records: builder, external parameters and resolved dependencies.

entry.title: Circuit breakers, from the fuse box to a Go service

link.title: Circuit breakers, from the fuse box to a Go service

entry.content:
A kitchen has one electrical circuit for the sockets on the counter. Someone switches on the kettle, the microwave and a heater at the same time. The wire in the wall now carries more current than it was made for, and it starts to get hot. A few seconds later, the breaker in the fuse box trips and the kitchen goes dark.

Nothing is wrong with the kettle. The breaker didn’t trip to protect it. It tripped to protect the wire in the wall, which would otherwise overheat behind the plaster where nobody can see it.

I studied electrical engineering before I moved to software. When I later worked on an experimentation service in Go, a circuit breaker in code was one of the patterns that felt familiar right away. It is a small piece of state in front of a call to another service. When that service keeps failing, the breaker stops calling it for a while and uses a fallback instead. This post explains why a busy service needs one, using the electrical version, and then walks through the code we used.

What goes wrong without one

The service answered one question per request: which variant of an experiment should this user see? It ran at around 5,000 requests per second on an average day, with a P95 latency under 100 ms. Each pod kept the experiment configuration in memory, with Redis shared between pods and the main config store behind it [8]. The breaker sat in front of the reads from that shared config layer.

Now picture the config layer having a bad minute. It doesn’t return errors. It just gets slow.

This is the dangerous case, and Little’s law shows why. The number of requests in flight equals the arrival rate times the time each one takes:

in flight = arrival rate × time per request

If a read normally takes 5 ms, then 5,000 requests per second keep about 25 reads in flight. If the same read now waits for a 1-second timeout, the same traffic keeps 5,000 reads in flight. The 5 ms and the 1-second timeout are only for illustration, not measurements. But the ratio is the point: the traffic didn’t change, the dependency only got slower, and the service is now holding 200 times more work.

Each request in flight holds a goroutine, some memory and often a connection from a pool. When the pool runs out, requests that don’t even need the slow dependency start to wait for a connection. Latency rises for everyone. Upstream services that call this one now wait too, and the slowness spreads. This is a cascading failure, and it is the reason Michael Nygard named the circuit breaker a stability pattern in Release It! [1].

A timeout alone doesn’t solve it. It limits how long one request waits, but every request still waits that long. The breaker is what stops paying that cost again and again.

The breaker protects the wire

Back to the kitchen. A breaker protects the circuit, not the device plugged into it [3]. The software version has the same split. It protects the caller: its goroutines, its connection pool and its latency budget. It also gives the struggling dependency room to recover, because the caller stops adding load to it.

That changes how you think about the fallback. While the breaker is open, the caller still has to answer the user. For us, the answer was the last configuration that worked. The previous post on this service describes the same rule: if the config store has a bad minute, assignment keeps working with the last known config [8]. For experiment assignment, a few minutes of old config is a fair price. A paused experiment may keep running a little longer, but no user gets an error.

Not every service can do that. A payment service can’t approve a payment from a cache. So the first question for any breaker is not the threshold. It is: what do we answer while it’s open?

Two ways to trip

A household breaker usually has two trip mechanisms in one box [3]:

  • A bimetallic strip handles overload. Current heats the strip and it bends slowly. A small overload trips the breaker after a delay. A short surge, such as a motor starting up, passes without a trip.
  • An electromagnet handles a short circuit. A very large current pulls it at once, with no delay.

The software breaker in hystrix-go has the same two kinds of protection, though the library doesn’t describe them this way.

The slow one is the error rate over a rolling window. hystrix-go keeps one-second buckets for the last 10 seconds [5]. It opens the circuit only when the window has at least 20 requests and at least 50% of them are errors [4]. One bad second doesn’t trip it, the same way a motor’s start-up surge doesn’t trip the bimetallic strip.

The fast ones work per call. A call that takes longer than the timeout fails at once. A call that arrives when too many calls are already running is rejected at once, without waiting. That limit is a bulkhead: it caps how much of the service one dependency can hold.

The recloser is the half-open state

A breaker in a house stays off until somebody walks to the fuse box. Power lines outdoors have something smarter: a recloser. On overhead lines, most faults are short. Lightning or a branch touching a wire causes a fault that is gone a second later. Of all faults on overhead distribution lines, 80 to 87% are transient like this [2]. So a recloser opens, waits a moment, and closes again by itself. If the fault is still there, it opens again. After a few tries, it stays open and waits for a crew. The standards allow at most four tries [2].

This is exactly the half-open state of a software breaker. After a cooldown, let a test request through. If it succeeds, close the circuit. If it fails, stay open and wait again.

The difference at the end is worth a thought. A recloser locks out because a fault that survives several reclosures is probably permanent, and closing again into a permanent fault does damage. hystrix-go never locks out. It sends one probe every sleep window for as long as the dependency is down. For a read from a config store, one probe every 5 seconds is harmless. For something expensive, a limit on retries or an alert after many failed probes would be the recloser’s lesson.

Selectivity: one breaker per circuit

A building doesn’t have one breaker for everything. Each circuit has its own, and the main breaker sits above them. They are chosen so that a fault in the kitchen trips the kitchen breaker and leaves the rest of the building on. Electrical engineers call this selectivity.

In hystrix-go, every breaker has a name, the command. Use one command per dependency, and sometimes per kind of call. If one breaker wraps both Redis and the main store, a problem in one cuts traffic to both. The Azure pattern page warns about the same thing: one breaker for several independent resources blocks the healthy ones too [7].

The code

Here is the shape of what we ran. This is a sketch with simpler names, not the original code. The numbers are the library defaults, not necessarily the values we ran with.

const cmdConfigRead = "config_read"

func init() {
    hystrix.ConfigureCommand(cmdConfigRead, hystrix.CommandConfig{
        Timeout:                1000, // ms per call
        MaxConcurrentRequests:  10,   // calls running at once
        RequestVolumeThreshold: 20,   // calls in the window before it may trip
        ErrorPercentThreshold:  50,   // % errors that trips it
        SleepWindow:            5000, // ms open before one probe
    })
}

Each field maps to one part of the electrical picture:

  • Timeout and MaxConcurrentRequests are the fast protection. A slow call fails after the timeout. A call over the concurrency limit is rejected at once with hystrix: max concurrency [6].
  • RequestVolumeThreshold and ErrorPercentThreshold are the slow one. Together they say: “trip only if there is enough traffic to judge, and enough of it is failing”.
  • SleepWindow is the recloser’s wait before it tries again.

The call itself:

func (s *Service) experimentConfig(ctx context.Context, id string) (Config, error) {
    // The run callback can outlive DoC's timeout. It owns its result and
    // sends it to a buffered channel, never to a shared return variable.
    result := make(chan Config, 1)
    err := hystrix.DoC(ctx, cmdConfigRead,
        func(ctx context.Context) error {
            c, err := s.store.Get(ctx, id)
            if err != nil {
                return err
            }
            s.lastGood.Store(id, c)
            result <- c
            return nil
        },
        nil, // handle the fallback below, on the calling goroutine
    )
    if err == nil {
        return <-result, nil
    }
    if c, ok := s.lastGood.Load(id); ok {
        return c.(Config), nil
    }
    return Config{}, err // nothing cached yet: surface the error
}

The callback is the normal path. It reads the config and, on success, saves a copy as the last good value. The caller handles the fallback after DoC returns an error: a failed read, a timeout, a full concurrency limit or an open circuit [6]. The error keeps the reason, so you can log hystrix: circuit open differently from a real store error.

The result channel has room for one value. On a timeout, the original callback can still finish and send without blocking, but it cannot overwrite the value returned by the fallback. Do not let the callback and fallback assign to the same captured variable: they can run concurrently. The store and the last-good cache must also be safe for concurrent access.

Two details in this code are easy to get wrong.

The fallback must be cheap and must not call the same dependency. Reading from memory is fine. Calling the store again “just once” from the fallback defeats the breaker.

The fallback needs a value to return. Right after a pod starts, there is no last good config yet. Then the only correct answer is the error. In practice the pod should load the config before it reports ready, so this case is rare.

Try it

The simulation below follows hystrix-go’s rules with the default settings: a 10-second window, 20 requests to judge, 50% errors to trip, and one probe every 5 seconds. Raise the failure rate and watch it trip. Then lower the traffic below 2 requests per second. The window never reaches 20 requests, so the circuit can’t trip at all, even if every call fails.

hystrix-go in slow motion

Each bar is one second: success, failure, short-circuited to the cache. Short-circuits count as errors in hystrix-go, and the window resets when the circuit closes.

circuit: closed answered by dependency: 0 answered from cache: 0

Closed: calls go to the dependency.

Things to watch

  • Low traffic never trips. With a volume threshold of 20 in a 10-second window, a command that gets one call per second can fail completely and stay closed. Set the threshold from the real traffic of each command, not from the defaults.
  • A timeout doesn’t stop the work. When hystrix-go’s timeout fires, it calls the fallback and frees the concurrency slot. The run function keeps running in its goroutine, and its result is thrown away [6]. Pass a context with a deadline to the store client too, so the slow call really ends.
  • Short-circuits count as errors. While the circuit is open, the rejected calls are counted as errors in the window [5]. This doesn’t keep it open, because a successful probe closes it and resets the window. But it makes the error rate on a dashboard look worse than the dependency really is.
  • Every pod has its own breaker. The state lives in memory. With 20 pods, each one has to see its own 20 requests before it trips. That’s usually fine and much cheaper than sharing state.
  • hystrix-go is old. Netflix’s Java Hystrix has been in maintenance mode for years and recommends resilience4j instead [9]. For new Go code, sony/gobreaker is a maintained option with the same three states and a configurable trip rule [10]. If you run a service mesh, Envoy’s outlier detection gives similar protection without code, by removing failing hosts from the pool for a while [11].

What carries over

I used the same pattern again recently, in front of LLM calls instead of a config store. The details changed: there, the fallback is a second model deployment instead of a cache, and there is no half-open state. I wrote that up in a separate post.

The questions to answer stay the same as for the breaker in a fuse box. What are you protecting? What happens to the user while it’s open? Can it tell a short surge from a real overload? And who closes it again, a person or a recloser? Once you can answer those four, the thresholds are the easy part.

References

  1. Michael T. Nygard, Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, Pragmatic Bookshelf. The book that named the circuit breaker as a stability pattern.
  2. Wikipedia, “Recloser”. Up to 80 to 87% of overhead line faults are transient; reclose attempts are limited to four before lockout.
  3. Wikipedia, “Circuit breaker”. Thermal-magnetic trip units, and the difference between a breaker and a fuse.
  4. afex/hystrix-go, settings.go. Default timeout, concurrency, volume threshold, sleep window and error threshold.
  5. afex/hystrix-go, metrics.go and rolling.go. The 10-second rolling window, and which events count as errors.
  6. afex/hystrix-go, hystrix.go and circuit.go. Fallback errors, the concurrency ticket pool, the timeout that doesn’t cancel the run function, and one probe per sleep window.
  7. Microsoft, “Circuit Breaker pattern”, Azure Architecture Center. States, half-open, and one breaker for several resources.
  8. From polling to push: getting experiment config to every service. The caching layers of the same experimentation service.
  9. Netflix, Hystrix README. Hystrix is in maintenance mode, with resilience4j recommended for new projects.
  10. Sony, gobreaker. A maintained Go circuit breaker with closed, open and half-open states.
  11. Envoy, “Outlier detection”. Removing failing hosts from a load-balancing pool for a growing time.

entry.title: Follow-up questions in a RAG chatbot: from the last message to a search query

link.title: Follow-up questions in a RAG chatbot: from the last message to a search query

entry.content:
An employee asks an internal chatbot: “How do I request a new laptop in Sweden?” The bot searches the company documents and answers. Then the employee types: “And in Poland?”

A person reads this as “How do I request a new laptop in Poland?”. A search index reads three words. It does not know the subject is a laptop, so it returns the pages that mention Poland the most. The answer is then written from those pages.

For a few weeks, a branch of our chatbot did exactly this. It already had a step that rewrites a follow-up into a full question before search. That step had a prompt, and the prompt had rules for follow-ups. However, after I changed how the conversation history was saved, the history it received was always empty. So every message was treated as the first message of a conversation. Nothing failed, and no error was logged. We found it before the change was merged.

Turning the latest message into something search can use is called query contextualization. Papers call it question-in-context rewriting [1]. This post goes through five levels of it, from no context at all to a rewrite that first decides what kind of follow-up it is. I moved the examples to an IT helpdesk, and I’ll leave out sizes and numbers that aren’t mine to share.

Level 1: search the last message

The simplest RAG chatbot sends each message to search as typed. For the first message of a conversation, that works. “How do I request a new laptop in Sweden?” has everything search needs.

It breaks on follow-ups, because people leave out what was already said:

  • “And in Poland?” keeps the subject and changes the location.
  • “Who qualifies for it?” points back with a pronoun.
  • “setting it up on my phone” answers a question the bot asked.

None of these can be searched alone.

Level 2: give the history to the answer model

The next idea is to send the earlier messages to the model that writes the answer. Chat APIs make this easy. Each request is stateless, so you pass the prior user and assistant messages yourself [7].

This helps the answer, and it does nothing for search. The model now knows the user means laptops. But the documents in front of it were found with “And in Poland?”. So it can refuse, or it can answer from the wrong pages. In a RAG chatbot the answer can only be as good as what search found. Therefore the history has to reach search.

In our chatbot, only the rewrite step reads the stored history. Search and the answer step get the rewritten query.

Level 3: rewrite the last message into a standalone query

Level 3 adds one model call before search. It reads the history and the latest message, and it returns a query that makes sense alone. For “And in Poland?” it returns “How do I request a new laptop in Poland?”. This is the task the CANARD dataset defines: rewrite a question that depends on the conversation into a self-contained question with the same answer [1].

Here is the shape of ours. This is a simplified sketch, not our exact code:

async def contextualize(message: str, history: list[Message]) -> Rewrite:
    if not history:
        # First message: only fix typos and extract a location.
        return await fix_and_extract_location(message)
    payload = json.dumps({
        "conversation": format_history(history[-10:]),
        "latest_user_message": message,
    })
    result = await llm.parse(
        system=REWRITE_PROMPT,
        user=payload,
        response_format=Rewrite,  # contextualized_query + locations
    )
    if result is None:
        return Rewrite(contextualized_query=message, locations=[])
    return result

A few choices in it are worth copying:

  • The first message skips the rewrite, because there is nothing to resolve. LangChain’s history-aware retriever makes the same choice. With no chat history, the input goes straight to the retriever [6].
  • The dialogue goes in as JSON in the user message, and the rules stay in the system message. The prompt says to treat the dialogue as data, not as instructions, and not to answer the question.
  • The output is structured: the query, plus the locations it names. A location becomes a search filter, so it should be a field.
  • If the model returns nothing usable, search runs on the raw message. A weaker search is better than no answer.
  • The rewriter keeps codes and acronyms exactly as written. A later step without a model expands the known acronyms, and it can only do that if the token is still there.

Level 3 handles most follow-ups. The cases it got wrong were less obvious. A generic rewrite prompt has one habit: when in doubt, add context. That habit is right for “And in Poland?”. It is wrong in several other cases.

Level 4: decide what kind of follow-up it is

Here is one of those cases. The user writes “I need help with VPN-7”. The bot asks: “Could you tell me more about what you need help with regarding VPN-7?” The user replies: “How do I reset my password?”

A generic rewrite sees a pending clarifying question and merges: “How do I reset my VPN-7 password?”. But the user has moved on. Their reply is a complete question with its own subject. If they had replied “setting it up on my phone” instead, merging would be right.

The two replies come right after the same bot message. Only the reply itself tells them apart. So before the rewrite chooses a subject, it has to decide what kind of follow-up the latest message is. These are the types our prompt separates. The examples are rewritten, but the rules are the ones in our prompt.

The latest message is Example Search with
A self-contained question, even right after a clarifying question "How do I reset my password?" the message as typed; copy nothing from earlier turns
A fragment that answers a clarifying question "setting it up on my phone" the pending subject plus the new detail
A bare topic after an ordinary answer "printer drivers" the topic alone, as a new query
A neutral follow-up with a pronoun "How long does it take?" the item the bot just explained
A complaint that the answer missed the request "Really nothing on it? Who qualifies for it?" the user's original subject
"Yes" or "no" to an option the bot offered "yes" the subject with the option applied, or dropped
A greeting, thanks or goodbye "thanks!" unchanged

A full question is not always standalone. “How do I apply?” is a complete sentence with no object. After an answer about the laptop loan program, it still needs that subject. Our tests have a case for exactly this.

Recency is not intent

The complaint type took the most attempts. Here is the shape of it. The user asks “Can I get a company phone?”. The bot answers: “I couldn’t find a company phone policy. I found the laptop loan program, which lends a laptop for up to two weeks.” The user writes: “Really nothing on it? Who qualifies for it?”

The nearest item to “it” is the laptop loan program. A rewrite that resolves pronouns by recency returns “Who qualifies for the laptop loan program?”. But the user is complaining that their own question had no answer. So “it” is the company phone, and the search should be “Who qualifies for a company phone?”.

The rule that fixed it says to resolve references using the whole latest message, not recency alone. If the user challenges the missing answer, every pronoun in that same message stays on the user’s original subject. The bot’s alternative is used only when the user names it or accepts it, as in “Who qualifies for the laptop loan you mentioned?”.

A neutral follow-up works the other way. After a normal answer, “How long does it take?” refers to the item the bot explained. An item the bot only mentioned in passing does not count.

Location is part of the follow-up

Location needs its own rules, because it often becomes a filter on search. An earlier location is inherited only by a related follow-up. If the user asked about laptops in Sweden and then asks “How do I book a meeting room?”, the new query gets no location. Our older prompt added an earlier location whenever the new query had none and the earlier one was clear. That narrowed unrelated questions to a country the user did not ask about.

The other rules are short. An explicit location in the latest message replaces the earlier one. A comparison keeps both locations. A location the user refused is never added back.

One bug here is easy to miss. The model mapped the language of a question to a country. A question written in Indonesian came back with Indonesia as its location, though no country was named. Our location prompt now says plainly that the language of a query is not a location.

Writing the rules as a decision list

Our first prompt for this step grew one fix at a time, and many lines had an exception such as “UNLESS it answers a clarifying question”. I rewrote it as one ordered list under the heading “Choosing the subject”. The order is the priority: when two rules seem to fit, the earlier one decides. The table above is that list, in the same order. The prompts post shows the prompt before and after the change, and how I tested it with repeated runs.

The prompt has only two examples, and both are analogous to the hard cases, not copies of test cases. At one point I added two more that matched the clarification tests almost word for word. I removed them in the next change. I prefer one general rule over a rule for each case, because case rules pile up and need changing later.

Try it below. Pick a conversation and step through the levels. Then switch off the history and look at levels 3 and 4 again.

One conversation, four levels

The queries are written by hand to show the typical behaviour at each level. They are not recorded model output.

CHAT
LEVEL
    SEARCH QUERY

    Level 5: keep the state outside the prompt

    Now the bug from the start. The rewrite step and its prompt were fine. The history it received was empty.

    We read the saved history from the agent framework’s context for the first agent, the one that runs the rewrite. The framework added the bot’s answer to that context only on the agent’s next call, and that call never came in the same turn. So every saved turn had a question and no answer, and the list of turns stayed empty. The fix builds each turn from the user’s message and the final answer that our own code already has, and passes the saved turns to the rewrite step as an argument. The post on state tells the full story, with a figure of the timing and the session schema.

    Two details matter for the rewrite step itself. It reads only the last 10 messages of the stored history, so each request stays at a known size. Every message you send counts against the model’s context window [7]. The number of restored turns also goes on the trace. A trace that says 0 restored turns on the third message of a conversation would have shown our bug much earlier.

    The general lesson: own the conversation state. Store it in your own schema, from values you control, and pass it in where it is needed. The framework’s internal context is a detail of how the framework calls the model. Its timing can change, and it is not a record of the conversation.

    Things to watch

    • An empty history looks like success. Without history, a follow-up still gets an answer, only a worse one. Put the number of restored turns on the trace.
    • Context added by default. A rewrite that always merges breaks new questions that follow a clarifying question. Test that case on purpose.
    • Recency resolving pronouns. A complaint refers to the user’s subject, even when the bot’s last answer named something else.
    • Location inferred from language. Say in the prompt that the language of a question is not a location.
    • Acronyms changed by the rewriter. Keep the token exact, and expand it in code. We also had to tell the answer step to keep an expansion like “ACRONYM (Full Form)” in its first mention, instead of shortening it back.
    • One more model call. The rewrite runs on the critical path of every follow-up. On the first message there is nothing to resolve, so we use a smaller call that only fixes typos and extracts a location.
    • Flaky prompt tests. Run each real-model case more than once, and decide in advance how many passes count.

    What others do

    The research on this is older than LLM chatbots. CANARD has about 40,000 conversational questions, each paired with a standalone rewrite [1]. In the TREC CAsT 2019 track, leading systems rewrote conversational queries with GPT-2. Queries resolved by hand still beat the best automatic system by about 35%, relative [2]. So the rewrite is a real source of lost quality, and it is worth measuring on its own.

    Rewrite-Retrieve-Read goes a step further and trains the rewriter [3]. A small model writes the query, and it is trained with reinforcement learning on feedback from the model that reads the results. Ours is a prompted model. Training one would need a set of follow-ups with good rewrites first.

    HyDE asks a model to write a hypothetical answer and searches with its embedding [4]. I tried it as a third search path in an earlier post: 0.6 points more recall for 2.4 times the retrieval latency. It solves a different problem. HyDE bridges the words of a question and the words of a document. Contextualization fills in what the user left out. A HyDE passage written from “And in Poland?” is still about Poland, so the rewrite has to come first.

    Multi-query retrieval asks a model for several versions of the question, searches with each, and keeps the unique union of the results [5]. LangChain’s default prompt asks for three versions.

    What I would try next

    • Search both readings when the type is unclear. For a complaint that might accept the alternative, search the original subject and the alternative, like multi-query, and let the reranker decide.
    • A golden set of follow-ups by type, taken from real traces and scored on the rewritten query alone. A wrong rewrite is cheaper to catch there than in the final answer.

    If your RAG chatbot answers follow-ups badly, check that the history really reaches the rewrite step before you touch the prompt. Then test a new question right after a clarifying question, and a complaint after a substitute answer. Those were the two cases our generic prompt got wrong.

    References

    1. Ahmed Elgohary, Denis Peskov, Jordan Boyd-Graber, “Can You Unpack That? Learning to Rewrite Questions-in-Context”, EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019. The CANARD dataset and the question-in-context rewriting task.
    2. Jeffrey Dalton, Chenyan Xiong, Jamie Callan, “TREC CAsT 2019: The Conversational Assistance Track Overview”, 2020. GPT-2 query rewriting in the top systems, and the gap to manually resolved queries.
    3. Xinbei Ma, Yeyun Gong, Pengcheng He, Hai Zhao, Nan Duan, “Query Rewriting for Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models”, EMNLP 2023. Rewrite-Retrieve-Read with a trainable rewriter.
    4. Luyu Gao, Xueguang Ma, Jimmy Lin, Jamie Callan, “Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels”, 2022. HyDE.
    5. LangChain, MultiQueryRetriever source. Several generated queries, and the unique union of their results.
    6. LangChain, create_history_aware_retriever source. Raw input to the retriever when there is no history, a generated search query when there is.
    7. OpenAI, “Conversation state”. Requests are stateless, you pass prior messages yourself, and long histories count against the context window.

entry.title: Running an agentic chatbot on Kubernetes when a request takes a minute

link.title: Running an agentic chatbot on Kubernetes when a request takes a minute

entry.content:
Before launch, we ran a load test on our chatbot. It is a multi-agent RAG service: one question goes through several agents, a search index and many model calls before an answer comes back. Under load, a single request took from half a minute to well over a minute. That is slow, but we expected it.

What we did not expect was the shape of the failure. Partway through the test, many requests failed with HTTP 503 in bursts. The pods were being restarted by Kubernetes. CPU and memory stayed low the whole time, so the autoscaler never added a pod. I’ll leave out the user counts and latency numbers, which aren’t mine to share.

The cause was a set of defaults that are fine for a normal web API. A normal API answers in milliseconds and burns CPU while it works. Our service answers in tens of seconds and spends almost all of that time waiting on the network. This kind of work is called I/O-bound: the limit is how many slow calls you can keep open, not how fast the processor is. This post goes through what that changed for us on Kubernetes.

How a probe restarted a healthy pod

Kubernetes checks each container with probes. A liveness probe asks “is this process stuck?” If it fails too many times in a row, the kubelet (the agent on each node) restarts the container. A readiness probe asks “should this pod get traffic right now?” If it fails, the pod is taken out of the Service, but it is not restarted.

Our liveness probe called GET /health every 15 seconds, with a 2-second timeout and 3 allowed failures. The endpoint itself is cheap. It returns 200 and checks nothing outside the process.

However, the pod ran one uvicorn worker, so one Python process with one event loop. That loop was handling many concurrent requests, each with long model and search calls. Waiting on the network does not block an event loop. Everything between the waits does: parsing responses, building prompts, framework bookkeeping, and any call that is synchronous by accident. With enough requests in flight, the loop could not get to the probe within 2 seconds.

Three failed probes, 15 seconds apart, is about 45 seconds. Then the kubelet restarted the container. Every request in flight on that pod died with it, and each of them had already used up to a minute of model calls.

The restart made things worse, not better. The new container needs time to start, and while it starts, its share of traffic goes to the other pods. Those pods get busier, their probes start to fail, and the same thing happens to them. The Kubernetes documentation warns about exactly this: a wrong liveness probe can restart containers under high load and cause cascading failures [1].

One limit to state here. At that time we had no metric for event loop lag, so I can’t say which piece of work kept the loop busy. We fixed the conditions around it, which I describe next.

Probes for a slow service

The first fix was to give each probe one job, and to make the liveness probe forgiving. This is close to what we run now:

startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8000 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 24     # up to 2 minutes to start
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8000 }
  periodSeconds: 30
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 5      # about 2.5 minutes of failures before a restart
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8000 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 5

The startup probe runs only while the container starts. Liveness and readiness wait until it has passed once [1]. So the slow start no longer needs a long initialDelaySeconds on the liveness probe, and the liveness probe can stay focused on one question: is the process stuck?

The liveness probe now allows about two and a half minutes of failures. That is longer than our slowest request. A loop that is busy for a minute is not stuck. It is working.

Colin Breck’s post on probes gives the same advice in more detail [2]. Keep liveness cheap and local, never check dependencies in it, and set its timeout close to your client timeout. He also points out that every restart puts more load on the other pods.

We also changed the pod to run more than one uvicorn worker. Each worker is a separate process with its own event loop, so one busy loop no longer means a silent pod. There is a trade-off here. It comes from my own reasoning, not from a measurement. A probe now reaches whichever worker accepts the connection. If one worker is truly stuck, the probe can still pass through another one, and liveness will not catch it. More workers also means more memory, and Prometheus metrics need multiprocess mode so the workers’ counters are added up correctly.

Shutting down without dropping answers

Probes are not the only thing that stops a pod. A rollout, a scale-down and a node drain all do too. When Kubernetes stops a pod, it runs the preStop hook, sends SIGTERM, and waits for the grace period. The default grace period is 30 seconds. After that, any process still running gets SIGKILL [3].

For an API that answers in 100 milliseconds, 30 seconds is plenty. For us it is shorter than one request. So we set a longer terminationGracePeriodSeconds and a short preStop sleep, which gives the gateway time to stop sending new requests before the process gets SIGTERM. On shutdown, the app drains its pending background writes with a bounded timeout, then flushes buffered trace spans before it exits. Without the flush, the last traces of a pod are lost, and those are often the ones you want to read.

Check the arithmetic for your own service. The grace period includes the preStop hook [3]. If your slowest request is longer than the grace period minus the hook, a scale-down can still cut an answer in half. When I last checked, ours was not fully covered.

Why the autoscaler did nothing

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) works from a ratio. It computes desired = ceil(current × currentMetric / targetMetric) [4]. For CPU, the metric is a percentage of the pod’s CPU request. With CPU as the only signal, the HPA can only react to work that uses CPU.

Our pods were full and idle at the same time. They had as many slow requests open as they could handle, and the processor was mostly waiting. From the HPA’s point of view, nothing was happening.

Our quick fix was to lower the CPU and memory targets, add a faster scale-up policy, and allow more replicas. It passed the retest, and production still runs on it. However, it is a stopgap. It scales on a side effect of load, not on load.

The signal that matches an I/O-bound service is the number of in-flight requests: requests that have started and not yet finished. It grows with both traffic and latency. If ten questions arrive each minute and each takes a minute, about ten are open at any moment. If the model gets slower, that number rises even when traffic does not, and that is exactly when you need more pods.

Try it below. Keep the traffic the same and make the model slower, then watch which signal moves. The numbers are an illustration, not our measurements: each answer uses 0.6 CPU seconds, and the target is 8 open requests per pod.

Same traffic, slower model

Open requests follow traffic times answer time. CPU follows only the work done, so it does not see a slower model.

open requests
CPU autoscaler wants
in-flight autoscaler wants

We haven’t built this yet. Here is the plan. The app already exposes Prometheus metrics, and the instrumentation library we use has an opt-in gauge for requests in progress [5]. KEDA is an operator that feeds external metrics to a normal HPA, so the HPA controller still does the scaling [6]. Its Prometheus scaler runs a query and compares the result with a threshold [7]. It also works with Azure’s managed Prometheus through workload identity [7].

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: chatbot-api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: chatbot-api
  minReplicaCount: 2
  triggers:
    - type: prometheus
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus:9090
        query: sum(http_requests_inprogress{handler="/query"})
        threshold: "8"   # in-flight requests per pod; pick yours from a load test

The threshold is the number of open requests one pod should hold. A load test is the way to find it: raise the load on a single pod until latency or errors climb, then stay well below that point. There is also a KEDA HTTP add-on that scales on HTTP traffic directly, through its own interceptor. It is still marked beta [8], so I would start with the Prometheus scaler.

Two leaks that only showed up under load

Neither of these is visible with one request at a time. Both appeared with many slow requests at once.

Model clients that were never closed

Each request built a fresh tree of agents, and each agent created its own model clients. Every one of those clients wraps an httpx connection pool. The agent runtime stopped at the end of a request, but stopping it did not close the clients. So every request left several connection pools open for the life of the process. Over time, that means more open sockets and more memory.

The fix closes them in a finally block, even when the request fails:

try:
    answer = await run_agents(question)
finally:
    for client in model_clients:
        try:
            await client.close()
        except Exception:
            logger.warning("failed to close model client", exc_info=True)
    await runtime.stop()

Each closing step has its own try, so a failure while cleaning up never hides the real error of the request. We also keep the clients in a list built at construction, so a renamed or newly added client can’t be forgotten in the cleanup.

The httpx documentation goes one step further [9]. To get the benefit of connection pooling, don’t create many client instances. Create one, share it, and close it when the app stops. A process-wide client per model deployment, closed in the app’s shutdown hook, would remove the problem instead of cleaning up after it.

A thread pool with six threads

Under burst load, reads and writes of conversation history to blob storage started to time out after 20 seconds. The traceback showed something odd. The time was spent before any network call had started.

The storage client uses aiohttp. With proxy settings taken from the environment, which the Azure SDK turns on by default, aiohttp looks up the proxy for every request in a thread through asyncio.to_thread. Token fetches from DefaultAzureCredential also run in threads. Both go to the event loop’s default thread pool. Its default size is min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4) [10]. On a pod with one or two CPUs, that is five or six threads.

So under burst, these small lookups queued behind each other, and the 20-second timeout ran out while they waited for a thread. The fix sets a larger default pool at startup [11]:

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    loop.set_default_executor(
        ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=settings.async_executor_max_workers)
    )
    yield

The size is a setting, so it can change without a code change. An async service still has threads in it. Libraries move small blocking calls onto the default pool, and you don’t see it until that pool is full.

Running the load test

Two things made the load tests useful, and both happen before the first request is sent.

Keep test traffic out of production data

The load test runs the full pipeline with the same models and prompts. Without care, it would also fill the trace store with thousands of fake conversations, and the online evaluators would score them as if they were real users.

So the API accepts a test header, X-Test-Mode: true. With it, the request gets a no-op tracer, so no spans are exported. Everything else still runs. The session store works as normal, because the test simulates multi-turn conversations. Conversation history is still written, because we wanted to load that path too. Each record is tagged is_load_test: true, so it can be filtered out or deleted later. The response also returns its own duration in a header.

A header that turns off tracing is also a way to hide traffic. Accept it only from inside your network, or require a secret with it.

Write the pass rule first

Before the retest, we wrote down what “pass” meant:

  • an error rate under an agreed limit
  • p95 and p99 latency under the gateway timeout
  • zero pod restarts during the run
  • the autoscaler adds pods within 2 minutes after the ramp ends
  • the first 2 minutes are ignored, because a burst start is meant to be rough

Writing it first stops you from reading a result as “good enough” after you see it. The latency rule is tied to the gateway. Our gateway route has a total request timeout, and a slightly shorter timeout for each call to the backend. The total must be at least as long as the backend timeout [12]. Any answer slower than that is a failure to the user, even if the pod finished it.

Locust can turn part of this rule into an exit code [13]. A listener on the quitting event reads the final stats and sets environment.process_exit_code, so a pipeline can fail on it:

from locust import events

@events.quitting.add_listener
def check_pass_rule(environment, **kw):
    total = environment.stats.total
    failed = (
        total.fail_ratio > MAX_ERROR_RATE
        or total.get_response_time_percentile(0.95) > GATEWAY_TIMEOUT_MS
    )
    environment.process_exit_code = 1 if failed else 0

Locust can’t see pod restarts or the autoscaler. Check those from the cluster: the restart count in kubectl get pods, and the HPA’s events in kubectl describe hpa. Also give your simulated users a think time between turns. People read a long answer before they ask the next question, and a test without that pause measures a different service.

Identity, briefly

Most of our pods’ calls to the model service, the search index and storage still use keys from Kubernetes Secrets. We have a written plan to move to workload identity on AKS. The pod’s service account token is exchanged for a short-lived Entra token, and each service grants roles instead of keys [14]. I described the same idea on GKE and Azure in an earlier post, so I won’t repeat it. One detail matters for this post: token fetches also run on that default thread pool. Size the pool before you add more of them.

Things to watch

  • A liveness probe stricter than your slowest request. A busy pod is not a dead pod. Restarting it throws away all the work in flight.
  • Dependencies in the liveness probe. If the model service is down, restarting every pod will not bring it back.
  • Readiness under load. Failing readiness when busy moves traffic to the other pods. That is fine if they have room, and a cascade if they don’t.
  • CPU as the only scaling signal. For a service that mostly waits, it measures the wrong thing.
  • A grace period shorter than a request. Every rollout and scale-down then cuts some answers.
  • Per-request clients. Anything that holds a connection pool should live as long as the process, or be closed in a finally.
  • The default thread pool. It is small on small pods, and libraries use it without telling you.
  • Histogram buckets. Default latency buckets often stop at 1 second. Make sure the top bucket is above your gateway timeout, or every slow request lands in +Inf.

What I would try next

  • Scale on in-flight requests with KEDA and a Prometheus query, as above, and remove CPU from the HPA.
  • Measure event loop lag. A small task that sleeps for a fixed time and records how late it wakes up shows how busy the loop is. asyncio’s debug mode can also log any callback that runs longer than slow_callback_duration, 100 milliseconds by default [15]. That would answer the question I couldn’t answer above.
  • Shared model clients per process, as the httpx docs recommend [9].
  • Workload identity, following the plan.

If you move an LLM service onto Kubernetes, start from the length of your slowest request. Set the liveness probe, the grace period and the gateway timeout around it. Then scale on open requests instead of CPU, and write the load test’s pass rule before you run it.

References

  1. Kubernetes, “Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes”. What each probe does, startup probes holding back the others, and the warning that a wrong liveness probe causes cascading failures under load.
  2. Colin Breck, “Kubernetes Liveness and Readiness Probes: How to Avoid Shooting Yourself in the Foot”. No dependencies in liveness, conservative timeouts, and restarts that add load to other pods.
  3. Kubernetes, “Pod Lifecycle: Termination of Pods”. The preStop hook, SIGTERM, the 30-second default grace period and SIGKILL.
  4. Kubernetes, “Horizontal Pod Autoscaling”. The scaling ratio, utilization as a share of the request, and custom and external metrics.
  5. prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator, README. The opt-in metric for requests in progress.
  6. KEDA, “Scaling Deployments, StatefulSets & Custom Resources”. How KEDA feeds metrics to the HPA.
  7. KEDA, “Prometheus scaler”. Query, threshold, and authentication to Azure Monitor managed Prometheus with workload identity.
  8. KEDA, HTTP Add-on. Scaling on HTTP traffic; project status beta.
  9. HTTPX, “Async Support”. Don’t create many client instances; close a client with async with or aclose().
  10. Python, “concurrent.futures: ThreadPoolExecutor”. The default max_workers and why it was chosen.
  11. Python, “Event Loop: run_in_executor and set_default_executor”. The default executor used when no executor is given.
  12. Envoy Gateway, “HTTP Timeouts”. The request and backendRequest timeouts on an HTTPRoute, and the rule that the request timeout is at least the backend one.
  13. Locust, “Running without the web UI”. Setting the process exit code from a quitting listener.
  14. Microsoft, “Use Microsoft Entra Workload ID with AKS”. Service account token projection, the OIDC issuer, and the token exchange.
  15. Python, “Event Loop: slow_callback_duration”. Debug mode and the 100-millisecond default for slow callbacks.
