Under load, a single request took from half a minute to well over a minute. That is slow, but we expected it.

entry.title: Keyword search, vector search, and the filter that runs first

link.title: Keyword search, vector search, and the filter that runs first

entry.content:
Say a user asks a chatbot: “How do I fix VPN error 809?” One chunk in the knowledge base is titled “Error 809: VPN blocked by the firewall”. Another is a long VPN setup guide that never mentions 809. A third is about error 806, a different problem with a similar number.

Keyword search finds the first chunk easily. “809” is a rare word, and that chunk contains it. Vector search compares meaning instead of words. To an embedding model, 806 and 809 can look almost the same, so the wrong error page may come first.

Now another user writes: “my laptop can’t reach the office network from home”. No chunk uses those words, so keyword search finds little. Vector search still finds the VPN guide, because the meaning is close.

Many RAG systems run both searches and merge the two result lists. This is called hybrid search. The multi-agent RAG chatbot I work on uses Azure AI Search in hybrid mode, with a reranker on top. I’ll explain how each of these parts works with one running example. Then I cover what caused us the most trouble, which was none of them. It was the metadata filter that runs before the search starts. I’ll leave out index sizes and numbers that aren’t mine to share.

Keyword search: BM25

Keyword search, also called lexical or full-text search, matches the words of the query against the words of each chunk. The usual scoring function is BM25, which comes out of the probabilistic relevance framework described by Robertson and Zaragoza [1]. Azure AI Search uses it for full-text queries [5].

BM25 scores each query term in each chunk and adds the scores up. Three things decide a term’s score. The first is term frequency: how often the term appears in the chunk. More is better, but each extra mention adds less than the one before. The second is inverse document frequency (IDF): how rare the term is in the whole index. A rare term tells you more than a common one. The third is length normalization. A long chunk matches more words by chance, so BM25 scales term frequency down for chunks that are longer than average.

score(q,d)=∑t∈qIDF(t)⋅f(t,d) (k1+1)f(t,d)+k1(1−b+b⋅∣d∣avgdl)\text{score}(q, d) = \sum_{t \in q} \text{IDF}(t) \cdot \frac{f(t,d)\,(k_1 + 1)}{f(t,d) + k_1 \left(1 - b + b \cdot \frac{|d|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)}score(q,d)=t∈q∑​IDF(t)⋅f(t,d)+k1​(1−b+b⋅avgdl∣d∣​)f(t,d)(k1​+1)​

Here f(t,d)f(t,d)f(t,d) is how often term ttt appears in chunk ddd, ∣d∣|d|∣d∣ is the chunk’s length and avgdl is the average length. k1k_1k1​ controls how fast term frequency saturates, and bbb controls how much length matters. Azure’s defaults are k1=1.2k_1 = 1.2k1​=1.2 and b=0.75b = 0.75b=0.75 [6]. The exact IDF formula differs a little between engines. The example below uses ln⁡(1+N−nt+0.5nt+0.5)\ln\left(1 + \frac{N - n_t + 0.5}{n_t + 0.5}\right)ln(1+nt​+0.5N−nt​+0.5​), where NNN is the number of chunks and ntn_tnt​ is how many contain the term.

Take an index of 1,000 chunks with an average length of 100 words. “vpn” appears in 200 chunks, “error” in 300, and “809” in only 3. That gives an IDF of 1.61 for “vpn”, 1.20 for “error” and 5.66 for “809”. Now score three chunks for the query “vpn error 809”:

Chunk Length Matching terms BM25 score
A: "Error 809: VPN blocked by the firewall" 50 vpn 1, error 1, 809 1 10.6
C: "Error codes, full list" 200 error 4, 809 1 5.8
B: "VPN setup guide" 300 vpn 6 2.4

The rare term does most of the work. “809” alone gives chunk A 7.1 of its 10.6 points. Chunk B says “VPN” six times and still gets only 2.4. With k1=1.2k_1 = 1.2k1​=1.2, one term can never add more than 2.2 times its IDF, and B’s length pulls it further down.

One detail is easy to miss. Azure AI Search splits an index into shards and, by default, computes these statistics per shard. Two near-identical chunks in different shards can then get different scores [5]. Our search call sets scoringStatistics to global, so IDF covers the whole index. It also passes a session id derived from the query, so all searches for one question try to use the same replica. The goal is an order that is stable from run to run, because that order is what the reranker receives.

Where keyword search fails

Keyword search needs the same words in the query and the chunk. A paraphrase, a synonym or another language scores zero. Acronyms are a case we hit in practice. A user types “WFH” and the document says “work from home”, or the other way around.

So before the query reaches search, the chatbot expands known acronyms from a small glossary. The query keeps both forms, for example “WFH (Work From Home)”, so keyword search can match either one. The glossary is keyed by acronym, then country, then language, because one acronym can mean different things in different countries. The model that rewrites the query is told not to expand acronyms, so this deterministic step is the only place it happens.

Vector search: embeddings and nearest neighbours

An embedding model turns a piece of text into a vector, a list of a few hundred or a few thousand numbers. Texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions. Closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity. At query time you embed the query and look for the chunk vectors nearest to it.

Comparing the query with every chunk is exact, but slow for a large index. So vector search engines use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) search. The common algorithm is HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World), from Malkov and Yashunin [2]. It builds a stack of graphs. The top layer has few points with long links. Each lower layer has more points with shorter links. A search starts at the top, moves greedily towards the query, then drops a layer and repeats. The paper reports logarithmic scaling with the size of the index. The result is approximate, so now and then the true nearest chunk is missed. Azure AI Search uses HNSW for its vector indexes [10].

In our call, the search service embeds the query itself and asks for the 50 nearest chunks.

Vector search is good at what keyword search misses: paraphrases, synonyms and, with a multilingual model, questions in a different language from the document. It is weaker on exact tokens such as error codes, product names, internal acronyms and numbers. Anthropic’s write-up on contextual retrieval puts it plainly: embedding models “can miss crucial exact matches”, and BM25 finds the specific string [11].

It also isn’t a safe default on its own. The BEIR benchmark tested retrievers on domains they weren’t trained for. It found that “BM25 is a robust baseline”, and that dense retrievers have “considerable room for improvement” in how they generalize [4]. An off-the-shelf embedding model reading your company’s documents is out of domain too.

Hybrid search: merging two ranked lists

You can’t merge the two lists by adding scores. A BM25 score has no upper limit, while a cosine score in Azure lies between 0.333 and 1 [7]. A sum would be decided by whichever scale happens to be larger.

Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) avoids the problem by ignoring scores and using only ranks. Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher proposed it in 2009 [3]. Each chunk gets one term for every list it appears in:

RRF(d)=∑r∈R1k+r(d)\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{1}{k + r(d)}RRF(d)=r∈R∑​k+r(d)1​

Here r(d)r(d)r(d) is the chunk’s rank in list rrr. The constant kkk softens the gap between rank 1 and rank 2. The paper fixed k=60k = 60k=60 in a pilot run and found that the exact value “was not critical”. Azure AI Search uses the same formula for hybrid queries, and its documentation names 60 as a good value [7].

Here is a worked example for our VPN query, with k=60k = 60k=60. Chunk A is the one that answers it.

Chunk Keyword rank Vector rank RRF score
A: Error 809: VPN blocked 1 3 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.0323
B: VPN setup guide 4 1 1/64 + 1/61 = 0.0320
D: Proxy error 806 3 4 1/63 + 1/64 = 0.0315
F: Laptop setup checklist 5 5 1/65 + 1/65 = 0.0308
C: Error codes, full list 2 none 1/62 = 0.0161
E: Home network tips none 2 1/62 = 0.0161

A wins, by a small margin. And F, which is 5th in both lists, ends up far above C, which is 2nd in one list. RRF rewards agreement between the lists. That is often what you want. It also means a mediocre chunk that both searches return can push out a good one that only one search found.

Try it below. Move kkk down towards 0 and watch the single-list chunks rise. Switch off one list and the fused order becomes that list’s order.

Fuse a keyword list and a vector list

Each chunk scores 1 / (k + rank) for every list it is in. The bar shows the part from the keyword list (blue) and from the vector list (orange). The ranks are the made-up example from the table above.

60

Keyword (BM25)

    Vector

      Fused (RRF)

        RRF isn’t the only option. Azure lets you give a vector query a weight, which multiplies its part of the score [7]. And when every list is scored on the same scale, for example by the same reranker, keeping each chunk’s best score can work better than fusing ranks. I compared the two for multilingual queries in an earlier post.

        A reranker on top

        Embeddings are fast because each chunk is embedded once, without ever seeing the query. A reranker reads the query and one candidate chunk together and scores how well they match. That is more accurate, and much slower, so it only runs on the top results of the first search. Nogueira and Cho showed early on that BERT, fine-tuned for this, works well as a passage reranker [14].

        In Azure, this step is the semantic ranker [8]. It takes the top 50 results of the BM25 or RRF ranking and gives each a score from 0 to 4. A 4 answers the question completely, a 2 is “somewhat relevant” and a 0 is irrelevant. Microsoft only says it uses multilingual models adapted from Bing. Two limits matter in practice. The reranker only reorders what it receives. It “can’t rerun the query over the entire corpus”, so a chunk that missed the top 50 stays missed. And the score distribution can shift a little between runs and model updates, so the documentation warns against fine-grained thresholds.

        We drop chunks below a threshold on the reranker score, so the model reads fewer, better chunks. My earlier post has the numbers on what the reranker did for us: recall barely moved, while the right page moved nearer the top.

        Our setup, and how it got there

        The first version of the chatbot used Azure’s agentic retrieval. In that managed feature, a language model plans the sub-queries and the service runs them. We replaced it with our own query planning and plain search calls. One reason was language: we couldn’t make the agentic version search in each country’s languages. In our offline comparison, the plain version found more of the right documents, ran about six times faster and cost about a tenth as much per question.

        The first replacement sent a keyword query with the semantic reranker on top, and no vector query. A later change by a teammate added the vector query to the same request, which made it hybrid. Here is the shape of the call today, simplified:

        results = await client.search(
    search_text=query,                      # BM25 side
    vector_queries=[VectorizableTextQuery(  # vector side, embedded by the service
        text=query, fields="content_vector", k_nearest_neighbors=50,
    )],
    filter=filter_expression,               # runs before both
    query_type="semantic",                  # reranker on the fused top 50
    semantic_configuration_name=semantic_config,
    scoring_statistics="global",            # IDF over the whole index
    session_id=session_id,                  # same replica for one question
    top=top,
)
chunks = [r for r in results if r["@search.reranker_score"] >= threshold]

        One question can fan out into several such calls, one per topic and language.

        The filter runs first

        Each chunk in our index carries metadata: a country, a region and a list of cities. The chatbot extracts the geography from the question and builds an OData filter from it. For a question about Sweden, the filter looks like this:

        ((country eq 'se' or country eq 'sweden') and (city/any(c: c eq 'common')))
  or region eq 'global'

        A filter is a yes or no test on each chunk. It has no score and no ranking. In Azure, a text filter only succeeds on an exact match, and string comparisons are case-sensitive [9]. For a keyword query, the filter runs before the search. For a vector query, the default on newer indexes is to apply it during the graph search, so you still get kkk results if that many pass [10].

        This makes the filter a quiet place to fail. If it removes the right chunk, no ranking can bring it back. Nothing throws an error either. The search still returns ten chunks, the reranker still scores them, and the model writes a fluent answer from the wrong sources. We had four such bugs, each in a different part of the filter:

        What went wrong Effect
        Documents for one country were tagged with two spellings of its name. The filter only sent the standard spelling. Most of that country's documents could not be found.
        The filter sent an upper-case country code, and the index held lower-case values. That clause never matched. The country name in the same filter still did.
        A refactor for city filtering dropped the region clause. Documents written for a whole region were not found for a question about one of its countries.
        A chunk with an empty city list was tested with city/any(c: c eq 'common'). any over an empty list is false [12], so dozens of documents for one office could never be found.

        I fixed the first one with an alias table, marked as temporary. A teammate fixed the second and the third. The fourth was found by a checker.

        None of these showed up as an error. So I built an index quality checker that runs on a schedule against each environment. It doesn’t copy the filter rules. It calls the real filter builder for every location a question can carry and reads the values back out of the generated filter. Then it checks that every document can be reached by the filter for its own country. It also reports when an alias in the temporary table no longer matches any document, so the alias can be deleted. The checker found the fourth bug, and it would catch a new spelling like the first one. Each search span in our traces also records the exact filter it used, so a wrong answer can be traced back to its filter.

        Chunks are not documents

        Search returns chunks, and one document is often split into several. One chunk of a file can pass a later relevance check while another is dropped. Our feedback triage once placed one file in three sections of the same report: “never retrieved”, “removed by the relevance check” and “used in the answer”. Each section was right about one chunk. Collapse chunks to a document identity before you count or report anything.

        Things to watch

        • If users type codes, product names or acronyms, keep a keyword side. Check how the analyzer splits tokens like “R&D” or “v2.1”.
        • Don’t add BM25 scores and cosine similarities. Fuse ranks, or normalize the scores first.
        • The reranker only reorders the top 50. If the right chunk is at position 80, the reranker can’t save it.
        • Test that every document can be reached by the filter for its own scope. Watch case, spellings, empty lists and clauses that a refactor might drop.

        What I would try next

        These are ideas from the documentation and from others’ work. I haven’t measured them on our system.

        • Add context to each chunk. Anthropic has a model write a short note that places each chunk in its document, and indexes it with the chunk for both BM25 and embeddings. With reranking on top, they report 67% fewer top-20 retrieval failures [11].
        • Move the glossary into a synonym map. Azure can expand query terms from a synonym map on a field [13]. The catch for us is that a field has only one map, and our acronyms differ by country.
        • Make filters ignore case. A normalizer on the filterable fields does this [9], which fixes the whole class of bug instead of one call site.
        • Tune the vector weight on a golden set, instead of leaving the default.

        If you are building search for a RAG chatbot, start with hybrid search and a reranker, and evaluate it on your own questions. Then spend as much care on the filter as on the ranking, and add a test that every document can be reached by the filter meant to find it.

        References

        1. Robertson, S. and Zaragoza, H. “The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond”. Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval, 2009. Where BM25 comes from, and the assumptions behind it.
        2. Malkov, Yu. A. and Yashunin, D. A. “Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs”. arXiv, 2016. The HNSW graph and its logarithmic search.
        3. Cormack, G. V., Clarke, C. L. A. and Büttcher, S. “Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperforms Condorcet and individual Rank Learning Methods”. SIGIR, 2009. The RRF formula, and the pilot that fixed k = 60.
        4. Thakur, N. et al. “BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models”. NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks, 2021. BM25 as a strong baseline out of domain.
        5. Microsoft, “BM25 relevance scoring”, Azure AI Search. Per-shard statistics, scoringStatistics=global and sessionId.
        6. Microsoft, “Configure BM25 relevance scoring”, Azure AI Search. What k1 and b do, and their defaults.
        7. Microsoft, “Hybrid search scoring (RRF)”, Azure AI Search. The RRF formula, score ranges per method, and vector weights.
        8. Microsoft, “Semantic ranking overview”, Azure AI Search. The top-50 window, the 0 to 4 score and its limits.
        9. Microsoft, “Text query filters”, Azure AI Search. Exact, case-sensitive matching, and normalizers.
        10. Microsoft, “Vector query filters”, Azure AI Search. HNSW, and prefilter against postfilter.
        11. Anthropic, “Introducing Contextual Retrieval”, September 2024. Why embeddings miss exact matches, BM25 plus embeddings with rank fusion, and reranking.
        12. Microsoft, “OData collection operators”, Azure AI Search. How any and all behave, including on an empty collection.
        13. Microsoft, “Add synonyms to expand queries”, Azure AI Search. Synonym maps, one per field, for free-text queries only.
        14. Nogueira, R. and Cho, K. “Passage Re-ranking with BERT”. arXiv, 2019. An early BERT reranker for passages.

entry.title: Keeping a chatbot answering when the model runs out of quota

link.title: Keeping a chatbot answering when the model runs out of quota

entry.content:
A user asks our chatbot a question. Before the answer appears, the backend makes about 15 model calls. It detects the language, classifies the question, rewrites it for search, filters what the search returned, and finally writes the answer. Most of these calls run one after another, and the chat window gives up after 60 seconds.

After launch, some of those calls started to fail with HTTP 429, Too Many Requests. Our own traffic was lower than we had planned for. However, the quota for a model is shared by every deployment of that model in the same subscription and region, and other deployments were using it too. When one of the 15 calls fails, the user gets no answer at all.

Two things helped. The first is a second deployment to fall back to. The second is a circuit breaker: a small piece of state that stops calling a deployment for a while when it keeps failing. This post goes through both, with the choices I made and the ones I would change. I’ll leave out quota sizes and traffic numbers, which aren’t mine to share.

Why a 429 is not always your fault

On Azure OpenAI, quota is counted in tokens per minute (TPM). It is given to a subscription per region, per model and per deployment type. Every deployment you create takes a part of that quota. So two teams that deploy the same model in the same subscription and region share one budget, even if their apps have nothing to do with each other.

The rate limit is also stricter than “tokens per minute” sounds. The quota documentation has two details that matter here [6]:

  • The token count is an estimate made when the request arrives. It includes max_tokens, so a request that asks for a large max_tokens uses budget even if the reply is short.
  • The requests-per-minute limit is checked over short windows, typically 1 or 10 seconds. A burst inside one second can get a 429 even if the minute as a whole is under the limit.

There are also two kinds of 429. One says rate limit exceeded: your deployment used its allocation. The other says the service is temporarily unable to process your request: the shared backend is short on capacity, and your quota did not change. The documentation says many people request more quota for the second kind, which doesn’t help. We log the two kinds separately for this reason.

Retrying the same deployment was not enough

The usual first answer to a 429 is to retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Backoff waits longer after each failure. Jitter adds a random part to the wait, so that many clients that failed at the same moment don’t all retry at the same moment too. Marc Brooker’s post explains why with a simulation [4]. The OpenAI Python SDK already does it: it retries twice by default and respects the retry-after header.

For us, retrying alone had two problems.

The first is time. A 429 often comes with a retry-after value of several seconds. The API Management documentation warns that it can be as large as a day [7]. With 15 calls in 60 seconds, each call has a few seconds to spare at most. Waiting for the same deployment to recover uses up the time the rest of the answer needs.

The second is that retries multiply. If the SDK retries twice and your own code retries twice around it, one failing call becomes nine requests. Google’s SRE book recommends retrying at one layer only, and keeping a retry budget per client [5]. A deployment that is out of quota also counts the rejected requests against its limit [6], so more retries make the throttling worse.

So I stopped retrying the primary. Its SDK retries are set to zero, and a different deployment takes the retry instead. A comment in the code says it in one line: the fallback is the retry.

A second deployment to fall back to

The fallback is a deployment of an older model that we already had quota for. Because quota is counted per model, it does not share a budget with the primary. Each kind of call has a primary and an optional fallback, set in configuration. If the fallback is empty, the primary runs alone with a longer timeout.

Not every error should fall back. The question to ask is: would another deployment probably succeed where this one failed?

These errors fall back:

  • connection errors and timeouts, including our own timeout per attempt
  • 404, which here usually means the deployment name is wrong or the deployment was removed
  • 408 and 409
  • 429, both kinds
  • any 5xx

A 400 does not fall back. A content filter rejection, for example, is about the input. The fallback would see the same input and reject it too, and we would have spent time for nothing. A bad output from the model does not fall back either, because the call succeeded. That is a quality problem, and it belongs to evaluation, not to this layer.

Here is the shape of it. This is a simplified sketch, not our exact code:

FALLBACK_STATUS = {404, 408, 409, 429}

def should_fall_back(exc: Exception) -> bool:
    if isinstance(exc, (APIConnectionError, TimeoutError)):
        return True
    if isinstance(exc, APIStatusError):
        return exc.status_code in FALLBACK_STATUS or exc.status_code >= 500
    return False

async def call_with_fallback(route, call):
    breaker = breakers[(route.primary.deployment, route.name)]
    if route.fallback and breaker.is_open():
        return await call(route.fallback)
    started = time.monotonic()
    try:
        result = await call(route.primary)
    except Exception as exc:
        if route.fallback is None or not should_fall_back(exc):
            raise
        breaker.record_failure()
        return await call(route.fallback)
    breaker.record_success(started)
    return result

call is a function that makes the request against one deployment. The same wrapper is used by the plain OpenAI calls and by the agent framework’s chat client, so there is one place where the rule lives.

A fallback has to fit in the time budget

A fallback only helps if it finishes before the user gives up. So every attempt has a hard timeout. The call that writes the answer gets 20 seconds on the primary and 30 on the fallback. The quicker calls get less.

Our first fallback for the answer ran at the same reasoning effort as the primary. In a test with the primary switched off, it took 42.6 seconds for one answer. Together with the other calls, that was over the 60-second limit. The fallback now runs at a lower reasoning effort. The answer is a little less careful, but it arrives.

These timeouts are per attempt, not for the whole request. A slow primary followed by a slow fallback can still go over 60 seconds. A deadline for the whole request, which every call checks before it starts, would be the cleaner fix. I haven’t built that yet.

The circuit breaker

The fallback fixed lost answers, but it left a cost. When the primary is out of quota, every call still tries it first. For a 429 that is a fast failure. For a timeout it is up to 20 seconds per call, spent waiting for something we already know is broken.

A circuit breaker removes that cost. The idea comes from Michael Nygard’s book Release It!, and Martin Fowler’s short article is a good introduction [1, 2]. It works like the breaker in a fuse box. While it is closed, calls go through and failures are counted. When failures reach a limit, it opens, and calls skip the failing deployment and go straight to the fallback. After a cooldown, calls try the primary again.

Ours is small:

TRIP_FAILURES, WINDOW_S, COOLDOWN_S = 2, 30.0, 60.0

class Breaker:
    def __init__(self):
        self.failures: list[float] = []
        self.opened_at = float("-inf")
        self.open_until = 0.0

    def is_open(self) -> bool:
        return time.monotonic() < self.open_until

    def record_failure(self) -> None:
        now = time.monotonic()
        self.failures = [t for t in self.failures if now - t < WINDOW_S] + [now]
        if len(self.failures) >= TRIP_FAILURES:
            self.failures = []
            self.opened_at, self.open_until = now, now + COOLDOWN_S

    def record_success(self, started: float) -> None:
        if started > self.opened_at:
            self.failures, self.open_until = [], 0.0

Two failures within 30 seconds open it for 60 seconds. One failure only sends that one call to the fallback. So a single slow answer that times out on a healthy deployment does not move all the traffic away.

There is one breaker for each primary deployment and each kind of call. A slow answer-writing call should not divert the quick classification calls, even when they use the same deployment.

The check in record_success is easy to miss. Calls overlap. A call can start on the primary, take 15 seconds, and succeed after the breaker has already opened because of other calls. Without the check, that late success would close the breaker right after it opened. So only a call that started after the trip can close it.

Try it below. Make the primary run out of quota, then switch the breaker off and compare how much time goes to failed attempts. Each dot is one call, one per simulated second. In this simulation the calls run one after another. Real calls overlap, so a slow failure would also hold up the calls behind it.

Break the primary and watch the breaker

Two failures within 30 seconds open the circuit for 60 seconds. A failed 429 costs about 0.3 seconds before the fallback starts. A timeout costs the full 20-second limit.

primary answered
0
failed, then fallback
0
skipped, circuit open
0
time lost on failed primary
0.0 s

Circuit closed: calls try the primary first.

With a 429 the breaker saves little time, because the failure is fast. With timeouts the difference is large: without the breaker, every call pays the full timeout before the fallback starts.

Where ours differs from the textbook

The usual circuit breaker has a third state. After the cooldown it goes half-open: it lets one or a few trial calls through, and only closes if they succeed [3]. Ours has no half-open state. When the 60 seconds are over, every call that arrives tries the primary again.

This works for us because the fallback still catches every failure. If the primary is still out of quota, a few calls fail and the breaker opens again after two of them. Those calls still get an answer from the fallback. The cost is a short burst of failed attempts every minute. For a deployment that is overloaded rather than out of quota, that burst could slow its recovery, and half-open would be the better choice.

The breaker state also lives in memory, one copy per pod. With several pods, each one trips on its own, so a broken primary costs two failures per pod instead of two in total. That is a known trade-off. Sharing the state, in Redis for example, would add a network call to every model call. API Management’s built-in breaker makes the same trade: its gateway instances don’t share breaker state either [7].

Prompts follow the model

A fallback is a different model, and a prompt tuned for one model is not always right for another. So each model has its own prompt file, picked by model name. There is a limit here. When a call falls back, it reuses the messages it already built from the primary’s prompt, so the older model runs on the newer model’s prompt. I would not assume that works for every pair of models. Test it with the primary switched off. The post on running several models covers the prompt files in detail.

Seeing fallbacks in traces

A fallback hides the failure from the user, and so it also hides it from you. If the primary has been failing all week, nobody notices unless the traces show it.

So every model call’s span records which deployment answered, and whether a fallback happened:

Attribute Example
llm.model_name the deployment that answered
llm.fallback.used true or false, always set
llm.fallback.reason RateLimitError (429), or CircuitOpen (...) when the breaker skipped the primary
llm.fallback.primary_latency_ms time spent on the primary before it failed

When the primary fails, the span also gets one llm.primary_failed event with the error. The span status stays OK, because the call recovered.

My first version did more. It added a child span for every attempt, so a healthy call had two spans instead of one. That added a cost to every healthy call, to show something that only matters when things go wrong. Attributes and one event on the existing span were enough. Now a healthy call adds nothing.

Grouping by llm.fallback.reason tells you what kind of problem you have. Timeouts and 5xx point to an outage, 429 to quota, and 404 to a wrong configuration. An alert on the fallback share, for example more than 5% of model calls in 15 minutes, tells you when the fallback is doing too much work.

Things to watch

  • Retries at two layers. The SDK retries by default. If you add your own retry or a fallback, set the SDK’s retries for the primary to zero, or one failure turns into many requests.
  • Same region, same problem. A capacity 429 is about the region, not your quota. A fallback in the same region can be throttled at the same moment. A second region or a global deployment type helps here, but data residency may decide whether you can use it.
  • A fallback that doesn’t fit. Measure the fallback with the primary switched off, end to end. Ours was too slow at first.
  • Falling back on the wrong errors. A 400 or a content filter error will fail on the fallback too.
  • A quiet fallback. Without an alert, a broken primary can stay broken for weeks.

What I would try next

Reading about how others do this showed me a few things ours doesn’t do yet.

  • Use retry-after for the cooldown. Our cooldown is always 60 seconds. A 429 tells you how long to wait. API Management’s breaker can take that value as its trip duration [7].
  • Different limits for different errors. The Azure pattern page suggests that timeouts may need more failures to trip than a clear “unavailable” [3]. LiteLLM’s router, for example, cools a deployment down on the first 429 and allows a few other failures before it does [8].
  • A half-open state with one trial call, if the primary is ever overloaded rather than simply out of quota.
  • Slow down before the 429. Azure returns x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens on every response [6]. A client could lower its pace when that gets small instead of waiting to be rejected.
  • A gateway instead of code. If several services share the same quota, a gateway puts the routing in one place for all of them. API Management with a priority pool and the LiteLLM proxy both do this [7, 8]. Doing it in the app has one advantage for us. The app also picks the prompt file and the reasoning effort for the fallback, and a gateway does not know about those.

If you call a hosted model from a service with a time limit, start with a short list of errors that may fall back and one retry layer. Give each attempt a timeout that fits the budget, and add a breaker that stops paying for a deployment that keeps failing. Then put the fallback in your traces, so you can see when it is doing the work.

References

  1. Martin Fowler, “CircuitBreaker”, 2014. The closed, open and half-open states, and credit to Michael Nygard’s Release It! for the pattern.
  2. Michael T. Nygard, Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, Pragmatic Bookshelf. The book that made the circuit breaker known as a stability pattern.
  3. Microsoft, “Circuit Breaker pattern”, Azure Architecture Center. Half-open behaviour, different thresholds per error type, and per-instance state.
  4. Marc Brooker, “Exponential Backoff And Jitter”, AWS Architecture Blog, 2015. Why retries without jitter still arrive in clusters.
  5. Alejandro Forero Cuervo, “Handling Overload”, in Site Reliability Engineering, Google, 2016. Retry budgets, and retrying at one layer only.
  6. Microsoft, “Manage Azure OpenAI quota”, Microsoft Learn. Quota per subscription, region and model; how the rate limit is estimated; the different kinds of 429; rate-limit headers; the SDK’s default retries.
  7. Microsoft, “Backends in API Management”, Microsoft Learn. Backend circuit breaker with acceptRetryAfter, priority pools, and breaker state that is not shared between gateway instances.
  8. LiteLLM, “Router: load balancing, fallbacks and cooldowns”. allowed_fails, cooldown_time, and an immediate cooldown on 429.

entry.title: Running several models in one LLM app, each with its own prompt

link.title: Running several models in one LLM app, each with its own prompt

entry.content:
In June we moved an internal chatbot to a newer model. The chatbot is a multi-agent RAG app, and one of its agents is a guardrail evaluator. Some replies, such as a clarifying question or a polite refusal, go through it before the user sees them. It checks each one against three rules. If a reply breaks a rule, the evaluator names the rule and the reply is rewritten.

In October I found that since the June change, it had flagged every reply it checked. The new prompt told the model to answer "none" when no rule was broken. The response schema did not allow "none". It listed only the three rules. With a strict schema, the model can only produce values the schema allows, so it had to pick a rule every time. Nothing raised an error, and no test failed.

The fix was one value in the schema. I replayed 14 captured replies and 6 synthetic unsafe ones, three times each. The false-positive rate went from 1.00 to 0.00 with the schema fix. Adding an example with "none" to the prompt, without the schema fix, changed nothing.

A model is more than a name in a config file. It comes with its own prompt, its own request parameters and its own way of following an output schema. When one app runs several models, each of these has to follow the model. This post is about the operations side of that: routing, prompt files, parameters, upgrades and traces. I’ll leave out sizes and numbers that aren’t mine to share.

Why one app ends up with several models

A deployment is a named instance of a model in your cloud account. You choose the name. On Azure OpenAI, quota is counted per model and region, so deployments of different models don’t share a budget.

One answer from our chatbot needs about 15 model calls. Most are short and structured: detect the language, classify the question, plan the search, filter the results. A few write longer text: the answer, the evaluators, and the step that turns a follow-up into a standalone question. These two kinds of call need different things. The short calls must be quick, so they run with reasoning switched off and a 10-second timeout. The writing calls need more care, so they run at medium reasoning effort with 20 seconds.

Each kind of call also has a fallback deployment of an older model, with its own quota. The fallback and the circuit breaker around it are covered in another post. Here the fallback matters for a simpler reason. It is a second model, and the app has to call it correctly too.

So the app has two routes, each with a primary and a fallback. Both primaries use the same newer model. What differs between the routes is the reasoning effort, the timeout and the fallback. In production that is three models behind four slots, where a slot is one primary or one fallback.

Routing per workload, set in configuration

Model routing is the choice of which deployment serves a call. In our app each call names a route, and the route comes from configuration. Each slot has three settings:

# names simplified
WRITING_DEPLOYMENT_NAME=chat-new-model
WRITING_MODEL_NAME=new-model
WRITING_REASONING_EFFORT=medium
WRITING_FALLBACK_DEPLOYMENT_NAME=chat-old-model
WRITING_FALLBACK_MODEL_NAME=old-model
WRITING_FALLBACK_REASONING_EFFORT=low
# and the same six for the short calls

An empty fallback deployment switches the fallback off for that route. Timeouts and retries stay in code. Deployments differ between environments, so they belong in configuration. The timeouts follow the 60-second limit of the chat window, which is the same everywhere.

The model name is set next to the deployment name on purpose. The deployment says where the request goes. The model name says what will answer, and the app uses it for two other choices.

One prompt file per model

Every prompt in our app lives in a TOML file, one section per agent. There is one file for each model:

Model Prompt file
the newer model its own file
the older fallback models one file each
any reasoning model without its own file a shared reasoning file
anything else the legacy file

The legacy file was written for the older, non-reasoning models. The reasoning file is about half its size: 497 lines against 951. Both cover the same agents.

Why not one prompt for all? Because models read the same prompt differently. OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 guide says that model follows instructions “more closely and more literally than its predecessors”, and that prompts written for other models “may not immediately work” [1]. The GPT-5 guide says that “contradictory or vague instructions can be more damaging” to the newer model than to older ones [2]. A fix that helps one model can hurt another. With one file per model, I can change the prompt for one model and know the others did not move.

Pick the file by model name, not deployment name

A deployment name can be anything. Our CI deployment once had a -cicd suffix, and a deployment could just as well be called prod-default. If the app picked the prompt from the deployment name, a rename in one environment would quietly load a different prompt. So the app picks by model name, and the model name is a required setting for every slot.

Here is the shape of it, simplified:

PER_MODEL = [
    (re.compile(r"new-model"), "prompts_new_model.toml"),
    (re.compile(r"old-model-mini"), "prompts_old_model_mini.toml"),
]

def prompt_file(model_name: str) -> str:
    if not is_reasoning_model(model_name):
        return "prompts_legacy.toml"
    for pattern, path in PER_MODEL:
        if pattern.search(model_name):
            return path
    return "prompts_reasoning.toml"

Two details are easy to miss. First, a prompt loaded without a model name gets the default file, which belongs to the primary of the writing route. Two short-call agents loaded their prompt this way. They ran on one model and read the prompt meant for another, until a fix passed the model name explicitly. Second, when a call falls back, it reuses the messages it already built from the primary’s file. So during a fallback, the older model reads the newer model’s prompt. We accept that, and we have run the app with the primary switched off to check it.

A new model’s file starts as a copy of the closest one. The file for our newest model is still that copy, with a comment at the top saying so. That is fine for a start. The point of the separate file is that it can now change without touching the others.

Keeping the prompt files in step

Several files that should define the same prompts will drift. One file gets a new section, the others don’t, and the code loads a section that is missing for one model. A short test stops that:

def sections(path):
    def walk(node, prefix):
        keys = set()
        for key, value in node.items():
            if isinstance(value, dict):
                keys.add(f"{prefix}.{key}")
                keys |= walk(value, f"{prefix}.{key}")
        return keys
    return walk(tomllib.load(open(path, "rb")), "")

def test_per_model_prompt_files_define_the_same_sections():
    reference = sections(REASONING_FILE)
    for path in PER_MODEL_FILES:
        assert sections(path) == reference, path.name

The test checks structure, not wording. Two other kinds of test check that the files agree with the code:

  • Examples in a prompt must parse into the response schema. Our intent classifier’s examples were missing a field the schema had gained, so a test now loads every example line from the prompt and validates it. It runs on both the legacy and the reasoning file.
  • Some rules must hold for every model. One example is “state the limitation first when the sources don’t answer the question”. A test asserts it in both the legacy and the reasoning file.

The test we didn’t have in June was the one from the opening story: every value the prompt tells the model to output must be allowed by the schema. That is a cheap test, and it would have caught three months of false flags.

Parameters that differ between model families

The same request can be valid for one model and rejected by another. Azure’s reasoning-model page lists the parameters that reasoning models don’t support: temperature, top_p, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty, logprobs, top_logprobs, logit_bias and max_tokens [3]. So one module builds the request arguments for every call, and it changes them by model family:

Parameter Older models Reasoning models What our code does
temperature, top_p, penalties accepted rejected dropped for reasoning models, with a debug log
output limit max_tokens max_completion_tokens renamed, and scaled up
reasoning_effort rejected accepted sent only to reasoning models
verbosity not available accepted sent through extra_body, because our SDK version had no argument for it
system message system system or developer system unless a setting opts in

The output limit is scaled because the limit for reasoning models covers reasoning tokens as well as the visible answer [3]. A limit that was right for an older model can cut a reasoning model’s answer short. Our code multiplies it by 2.5, with a floor of 4,096 tokens.

Sending a parameter or omitting it

An empty reasoning effort in our configuration means the app does not send the parameter at all. Omitting a parameter is a real choice. It means “use this model’s default”, and the default changes between models. Azure’s page notes that one model version changed its default effort to none. Code that relied on the old default would get no reasoning after that upgrade [3]. The span records not-sent in that case, so a trace never shows a default that we did not choose.

A wrong value is worse than a missing one. Azure answers an unknown effort with a 400. A 400 does not trigger our fallback, because it is about the request. So a typo in the effort setting would break every call on that route. The settings now reject an unknown effort when the app starts.

When the app can’t tell the family

The family comes from the model name, matched against patterns. If the name doesn’t match, the code assumes the older family. A comment in the code explains why:

Misclassifying a reasoning deployment as legacy fails fast with a clear “Unsupported parameter” 400; the reverse silently drops parameters the caller expected.

I like this rule. An error you see on the first request is better than a wrong answer you find a month later. There is also a setting to force the family, for a deployment whose name says nothing about the model.

The patterns are not a permanent truth. The same Azure page now lists a newer model family that supports temperature again [3]. A rule like “reasoning models reject temperature” is true for a set of models, not forever.

Try it below. Pick an environment and a slot, and see what the app would send. Then switch the prompt key to the deployment name, or pick an empty or misspelled effort.

Build one model call

The settings are a simplified version of the configuration above. All names are made up.

ENVIRONMENT
SLOT
PICK PROMPT BY
DEPLOYMENT
PROMPT FILE
REQUEST ARGUMENTS
LLM SPAN
RESULT

Structured output

Every model we use supports structured output, so the schema is the same for all of them. The agent framework still asks the app to declare what a model supports, such as JSON and structured output. We declare it once for all deployments. The opening story is the other half of this. A strict schema always wins over the prompt. If the prompt and the schema disagree, the model follows the schema, and nothing tells you.

Keeping the old model working

When we first moved to a reasoning model, a teammate’s change kept the older models working beside it. The compatibility module and the first reasoning prompt file came from that change. Because of it, moving back is a configuration change. Every slot can point at an older model, and the request and the prompt follow.

Backward compatibility also has a cost. Until October, the default in our CI workflow still pointed the model tests at an older model, while production had used the newer one since June. Unless a repository setting overrode that default, those tests checked a different prompt file from the one users got. Keeping the old path working made that easy to miss.

An upgrade is a prompt change and an eval

In production, our June move to the newer model was a four-line configuration change. The prompt file for that model already existed. However, nothing in our tests compared that prompt with the response schemas, and nothing ran the model tests on the new model. That is how the evaluator bug lasted three months.

So now I treat an upgrade as three steps:

  1. Give the new model its own prompt file, copied from the closest one, and tune it there.
  2. Run the eval set with the new model as the primary, and compare it with the current model on the same questions. Run the contract tests on the new file too.
  3. Switch the configuration, and keep the current model as the fallback for a while. Rolling back is then a configuration change.

Azure’s model lifecycle page gives the same advice for a retiring model. Evaluate candidates “against your own application, prompts, and representative data”, and compare quality, latency and cost together [4]. The same page has a warning for anyone who thinks of a deployment name as fixed. Standard deployments are upgraded automatically when a model version retires, and the deployment’s versionUpgradeOption decides when, or whether, that happens [4]. An upgrade like that changes the model without any change in your repository.

Seeing which model answered

With several models and a fallback, “which model answered this?” is a question you will ask often. In June a teammate fixed two agents’ spans that showed no useful model name. Now every routed call writes these on its existing LLM span:

Attribute Example
llm.model_name the deployment that answered
llm.route the route the call used
llm.reasoning_effort none, medium, or not-sent

With these, you can compare p95 latency by model and by route. The same span also records whether a fallback answered, which the post on quota and fallbacks covers. OpenTelemetry’s GenAI conventions make a distinction that I find useful here. gen_ai.request.model is the model you asked for, and gen_ai.response.model is “the name of the model that generated the response” [5]. Our llm.model_name holds a deployment name, so it can’t show an automatic version upgrade.

Things to watch

  • Prompt and schema disagree. Test that every value the prompt asks for is allowed by the schema. A strict schema overrides the prompt without an error.
  • The wrong key for the prompt. Pick the prompt file by model name. Make the model name a required setting, even when it equals the deployment name today.
  • A call site with no model. A default prompt file is convenient, and it is wrong for every agent on a different model.
  • Omitted parameters. An omitted parameter takes the model’s default, and defaults change between versions. Record what you sent.
  • Bad values that don’t fall back. A 400 from a typo in a setting breaks the whole route. Validate settings when the app starts.
  • Tests on a different model. If CI runs another model, it also loads another prompt file.

What others do

A few ideas from outside that I haven’t built:

  • A router library or gateway. LiteLLM can drop the parameters a model does not support. By default it raises an error instead, and you opt in to dropping with drop_params [6]. Our code drops sampling parameters for reasoning models with only a debug log. One option is to raise in tests and drop in production, so a parameter that someone expects to work fails early.
  • Model settings stored with the prompt. Langfuse lets each prompt version carry a config object with the model name and parameters, “versioned together with the prompt” [7]. In our app the prompt is in a TOML file and the effort is in environment settings, so a change can touch one and forget the other.
  • Evals on every change. OpenAI’s evaluation guide suggests continuous evaluation, which runs evals on every change [8]. A model upgrade is one of those changes, and a prompt edit for one model is another.
  • The model that answered, from the response. Record the response model next to the requested one, as the OpenTelemetry conventions suggest [5]. An automatic upgrade would then show up in traces.

If your app calls more than one model, give each model its own prompt file and pick it by model name. Test that the files agree with each other and with your schemas. Then treat the next model upgrade as a prompt change with an eval, and keep the old model ready as a fallback until the new one has proven itself.

References

  1. OpenAI, “GPT-4.1 Prompting Guide”, OpenAI Cookbook. More literal instruction following, and why existing prompts may need migration.
  2. OpenAI, “GPT-5 prompting guide”, OpenAI Cookbook. Why contradictory or vague instructions hurt the newer models more; reasoning_effort and verbosity.
  3. Microsoft, “Azure OpenAI reasoning models”, Microsoft Learn. Unsupported parameters, max_completion_tokens covering reasoning tokens, developer messages, and default reasoning effort per model.
  4. Microsoft, “Foundry Models lifecycle and support policy”, Microsoft Learn. Retirement, automatic upgrades, versionUpgradeOption, and evaluating a replacement on your own data.
  5. OpenTelemetry, “Semantic conventions for generative client AI spans”. gen_ai.request.model and gen_ai.response.model.
  6. LiteLLM, “Drop Unsupported Params”. Raising by default, and drop_params to drop instead.
  7. Langfuse, “Prompt Config”. Model name and parameters versioned with the prompt.
  8. OpenAI, “Evaluation best practices”. Continuous evaluation on every change.

entry.title: From a multi-agent group chat to one agent with fixed steps

link.title: From a multi-agent group chat to one agent with fixed steps

entry.content:
Our chatbot has an agent called the Orchestration Agent. It reads the JSON that the reception agent wrote and copies five fields into a new JSON. Then it adds one more field: the name of the agent that should speak next. That name is always the same. The Orchestration Agent never calls a model.

It is one of about a dozen agents in three nested group chats. In each group chat, a selector function decides who speaks next. Two of those functions carry the same comment: the selection is deterministic, to avoid LLM calls.

So we had built a multi-agent system, and then written a lot of code to make sure the agents did not decide anything. This post goes through that gap. It covers the difference between a workflow and an agent, what the group chat cost us, and how we are moving to one agent whose steps are fixed in code. I’ll leave out sizes and numbers that aren’t mine to share.

Workflows and agents

Anthropic’s post on building effective agents gives each side one sentence [1]. Workflows are “systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths.” Agents are “systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage.”

I reduce that to one question: who decides the next step? If your code decides, it is a workflow, even when every step calls a model. If the model decides, it is an agent.

So a step that asks a model “is this question in scope?” and then routes on the answer in code is still a workflow. Anthropic calls this pattern routing: it “classifies an input and directs it to a specialized followup task” [1]. The model classifies. The code owns the edge.

Microsoft’s Agent Framework documentation puts the choice in a table [3]. Use an agent when the task is open-ended or conversational, or needs autonomous tool use and planning. Use a workflow when the process has well-defined steps and you need explicit control over the order. Below the table is one line I like: “If you can write a function to handle the task, do that instead of using an AI agent.”

OpenAI’s guide is even stricter [2]. Apps that use LLMs but don’t let them control the workflow are not agents in its definition. Its examples are “simple chatbots, single-turn LLMs, or sentiment classifiers”.

How the chatbot was built

The chatbot answers questions from internal documents. It was built in 2025 on AutoGen, as three nested group chats. A reception chat works out what the user is asking. If the question is clear, it passes it to a RAG chat that searches and filters documents. The RAG chat passes the documents to a response chat that writes the answer and checks it. Each inner chat is wrapped as a single agent inside the chat above it.

Each group chat is an AutoGen SelectorGroupChat. By default it asks a model to pick the next speaker. The model reads the conversation and the agents’ descriptions, then names an agent [4]. You can also pass your own selector_func. If it returns a name, that agent speaks. If it returns None, AutoGen falls back to the model [4].

Here is the shape of our RAG chat’s selector. This is a simplified sketch, not our exact code:

def select_next(messages):
    last = messages[-1]
    if last.source == "Filter_Agent":
        sources = json.loads(last.content)["sources"]
        if not sources:
            return "Retrieval_Agent" if retries_left() else "Reply_Agent"
        return "Response_Agent"
    if last.source in ONLY_NEXT:  # exactly one allowed next speaker
        return ONLY_NEXT[last.source]
    return None                   # AutoGen asks the model

Every path we know about returns a name. The model is only there for a case nobody planned. So the flow was a fixed graph all along. We had written it by hand, inside a callback whose job was to name the next speaker.

Try it below. Pick a question and step through one turn in both designs. The paths are a simplified sketch of our chatbot, not its exact agents.

One turn, two designs

Top: the group chat, where a selector names the next speaker after every message. Bottom: one agent with fixed steps, where code calls the next function.

QUESTION
USER
GROUP CHAT
    ONE AGENT, FIXED STEPS
      next-speaker decisions
      0
      hidden model picks
      0
      fixed steps run
      0

      What the group chat cost us

      The group chat worked, and it answered users for a long time. But it made a fixed flow hard to read and hard to change. Here is where that showed.

      The routing was spread out. Each selector also updates counters, such as how many clarifying questions the bot has asked in a row. To answer “why did this user get a fallback?”, you follow the messages through three selectors and the counters they change.

      The limits were easy to get wrong. Each group chat has max_turns=25, but the limits that matter are the counters. One clarifier ran after the answer was written, when the answer scored low on relevance. In one dev session it asked four clarifying questions in a row. The reception chat reset its counter on every reply from the RAG chat, so nothing capped the loop. We removed that clarifier. A low-relevance turn now returns the answer, its source links, and a line that tells the user where to get help from a person.

      The fallback to a model was invisible. All three selectors are given a small model, and their calls are made outside our LLM spans. Our model router does not trace them, to avoid orphan traces. So if a selector ever fell through to the model, we would pay for a call we could not see.

      Agents passed data as text. Each agent writes JSON into a chat message, and the next agent parses it with json.loads. The Orchestration Agent reads the last message, and if that one is not from reception, it reads the one before. The shape of the data between steps lived in prompts and parsing code, not in a type.

      The framework’s state leaked into ours. At first, the session store kept the raw output of the team’s save_state(). A change of framework would have broken every live conversation.

      Moving to a workflow, one seam at a time

      We didn’t start with a rewrite. The first step was a seam: an interface the rest of the code depends on, so the implementation behind it can change. A decision record we wrote in July 2026 says it directly: decouple the code from AutoGen now, and decide about a migration later, with its own evidence.

      A handful of small pull requests did this. They removed dead code and replaced AutoGen’s token-usage types with our own. They also wrapped the session state in a versioned envelope, and put an interface between the API route and the group chats:

      class ConversationOrchestrator(Protocol):
    async def run(
        self,
        query: str,
        session_state: dict[str, object],
        *,
        context: OrchestrationContext,
    ) -> OrchestrationResult: ...

      The route now depends on this protocol only. Its tests use a fake orchestrator and don’t start any agents. A later change replaced the framework’s state with our own small schema: a few counters and the last eight turns. This work is merged. It was useful whether or not we ever changed frameworks.

      The first port did too much

      The first port to Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) came the same month, on a branch. It replaced the three group chats with one flat graph. In MAF, the nodes of a graph are executors and the connections are edges [7]. Reception became the start executor, routing decisions moved to switch-case edges, and every path ended in one terminal executor.

      The shape was right. However, the same branch also changed prompts, merged four reception calls into one, and changed how clarification worked. It added an adapter, a runner and a message type for each stage. In an offline eval, answer quality was about the same as before, and latency did not go down.

      When a port changes the framework and the behavior together, an eval cannot tell you which change moved a result. Meanwhile the main branch moved on. The pull request was closed in October without merging. The new plan builds from the current code and uses the old branch only as a source of ideas and test cases. It also tags every eval case as either preserved or intentionally changed.

      The current plan is smaller

      The plan from October 2026 has three executors: receive, retrieve and respond. Each one calls ordinary Python functions, and the business rules live in those functions. No model picks the next step. In MAF the workflow is wrapped as a single agent, so the rest of the app talks to one agent instead of a team.

      Its first draft didn’t use a graph at all. It recommended a plain Python coordinator, something like this sketch:

      async def run_turn(query, state):
    request = await receive(query, state)   # understand, check scope
    if request.reply:                       # greeting, clarification, refusal
        return request.reply
    sources = await retrieve(request)       # plan, search, filter
    if not sources:
        return no_answer(request)
    return await respond(request, sources)  # write, check, cite

      The graph won in the end, for reasons the plan writes down. MAF gives each executor its own span in our traces, and a graph follows the framework’s own guidance. The plan also names the cost. Each executor must either send one input to the next step or yield one final result, never both. A guard then checks that exactly one result came out. A plain chain of functions needs neither rule.

      This work is still on a branch as I write this.

      What a new orchestrator does not fix

      We expected the first port to make answers faster. It didn’t. When I broke turn latency down by what each turn did, most of the time went to the model writing the answer. Most of the rest grew with the number of documents retrieved. The orchestration itself was a small fixed part.

      So change the orchestration to make the flow readable and testable, and to stop paying for routing calls. Don’t change it to make the model write faster. For that, the length of the answer matters much more.

      Where an agent fits

      None of this means agents are a mistake. Anthropic’s post says agents fit “open-ended problems where it’s difficult or impossible to predict the required number of steps, and where you can’t hardcode a fixed path” [1]. The same post warns that agentic systems “often trade latency and cost for better task performance”.

      OpenAI’s guide lists where agents earn their place [2]. One case is decisions that need judgment and have many exceptions. Another is rule sets that have become too hard to maintain. A third is work that depends heavily on unstructured data. Then it says: “Otherwise, a deterministic solution may suffice.”

      In our chatbot, the model has real freedom in one place: the text of the answer. The other model calls classify, rewrite queries or filter documents, and code acts on what they return.

      If you do need an agent, start with one. OpenAI’s guide recommends that you “maximize a single agent’s capabilities first” [2]. It suggests splitting only when prompts fill up with if-then-else branches, or when the agent keeps choosing the wrong tool among overlapping ones.

      Two sides of the multi-agent debate

      Two posts from June 2025 are worth reading together. Cognition’s “Don’t Build Multi-Agents” argues from two principles [5]. Share full context between agents, and remember that “actions carry implicit decisions”. In their example, two subagents each build part of a Flappy Bird clone. One builds a background that looks like Super Mario Bros., and the other builds a bird that doesn’t match it. Their advice is a single-threaded linear agent.

      A day later, Anthropic described its multi-agent research system [6]. Parallel subagents search different directions at once, which helps on broad research questions. The post is also clear about where this does not fit: tasks where all agents need the same context, or with many dependencies between agents. I summarized its checklist in a note on multi-agent systems.

      The two posts agree more than their titles suggest. Split work across agents only when the parts are independent. A chatbot turn is the opposite case, because each step needs what the step before it produced.

      Questions before you add an agent

      • Can you draw the flow before you see the input? Write it as code.
      • Is the decision a choice from a fixed list? Use one model call with structured output, and route on the answer in code.
      • Does the next step depend on results you can’t predict, like a search that may need several tries? Use one agent with tools and a turn limit.
      • Do the parts run in parallel, need separate context, and rarely depend on each other? Then consider several agents, and measure the extra tokens against an eval.

      Things to watch

      • A class called an agent that never calls a model is a function. Call it one, so readers don’t look for a prompt.
      • If a selector can return None, a missing case quietly becomes a model call. In a fixed flow, raise an error instead.
      • A turn limit per group chat does not stop a loop that spans several user turns. Count the thing you want to cap, and reset the count only where that thing really ends.
      • Don’t store a framework’s internal state in your session store. Store your own schema, with a version number.
      • Porting to a new framework and changing behavior in one release makes the eval hard to read. Keep them apart, or label each eval case.
      • Measure where the time goes before you rewrite the orchestrator for speed.

      If the flow of your chatbot fits on a whiteboard before any user types a question, write it as a workflow. Use the model for the steps that need language, and keep the decision about what happens next in code you can test.

      References

      1. Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang, “Building effective agents”, Anthropic, 2024. The workflow and agent definitions, the routing pattern, when agents fit, and the advice to start with the simplest solution.
      2. OpenAI, “A practical guide to building agents”. What counts as an agent, when to build one, and maximizing a single agent before splitting.
      3. Microsoft, “Microsoft Agent Framework overview”, Microsoft Learn. The table of when to use agents and when to use workflows.
      4. Microsoft, “Selector Group Chat”, AutoGen documentation. Model-based speaker selection, and the fallback to it when selector_func returns None.
      5. Walden Yan, “Don’t Build Multi-Agents”, Cognition, 2025. Sharing context, implicit decisions in actions, and the single-threaded linear agent.
      6. Anthropic, “How we built our multi-agent research system”, 2025. Where parallel subagents help, and where shared context and dependencies make them a poor fit.
      7. Microsoft, “Workflow builder and execution”, Microsoft Learn. Executors, edges and the superstep model in MAF workflows.
